It explains that this core group would allow anti-LGBTQ+ and anti-abortion governments to collaborate on “coordinated voting” to “dilute, block, or impose conditions on language regarding sexual and reproductive health and rights.” The briefing also predicts that the core group would accelerate existing efforts to portray anti-LGBTQ+ politics as “sovereign resistance” against “globalism” in the public eye. “This discourse … asserts national sovereignty over agreed-upon international human rights, reframing sexual and reproductive rights as an external imposition rather than as already recognized human rights standards,” the briefing reads. How did we get here? The first CIVF, held in Mexico City in 2017. Image from CIVF via Wikimedia Commons. CC BY-SA 4.0 . Lara is the founder and president of the Ibero-American Congress for Life and Family (CIVF). Founded in Mexico City in 2017, CIVF describes itself as “ Un movimiento de reforma moral, educativa, social y jurídica por la vida y la familia” ( a movement for moral, educational, social, and legal reform for life and family) and is best known for holding an annual congress for leaders, primarily from Latin America and Spain, to discuss the promotion of socially conservative policies. In a 2021 article in an evangelical publication, Lara said that his group had applied to become a core group at the U.N. “We have the conviction that it is our responsibility as believers to be a light in the midst of darkness, this is why [we] are making this big effort,” he said. The third CIVF, held in Panama in 2019. Image from CIVF via Wikimedia Commons. CC BY-SA 4.0 . While that application never came to fruition, Lara remained interested in starting a U.N. core group, and announced in July 2026 that CIVF — which did not respond to Uncloseted Media’s request for comment — was launching a new plan to do so. How did the US get involved? The following month, Lara shared more details of the plan with The Washington Stand, a news outlet owned by Family Research Council , a Southern Poverty Law Center-designated anti-LGBTQ hate group closely affiliated with Focus on the Family . In the article, Lara says the goal is for the U.S. to sponsor the new group because of its powerful position on the world stage. Sjödin is concerned about U.S. involvement in a group like this. “[It] already has an outsized influence on the world, so the U.S. potentially taking on a leadership role in a coalition like this also risks the effects being outsized and makes this an initiative that is going to be more difficult to challenge,” she says. Valerie Huber speaking at CPAC Hungary in 2022. Image by Elekes Andor via Wikimedia Commons . CC BY-SA 4.0 . To that end, CIVF enlisted Valerie Huber, an influential American ally based in Washington, D.C., in their fight. Huber, who co-led the September 17th forum alongside Lara, is an American right-wing activist who held multiple leadership roles at the Department of Health and Human Services (HHS) during Trump’s first term. She has consistently promoted the exclusion of LGBTQ+ people in her work — the organization she led before getting her HHS appointment released a guideline that said “it would be inappropriate and unethical to assert or affirm” trans kids’ genders. “Valerie Huber is internationally recognized in the anti-rights space,” Wendy Via, co-founder and president of the Global Project Against Hate and Extremism , told Uncloseted Media. “She is bringing some credibility [and] influence to the idea of creating a separate core group, so she’s gonna be able to get people to join with her.” During her tenure at HHS, Huber helped craft the Geneva Consensus Declaration on Promoting Women’s Health and Strengthening the Family (GCD), an agreement between 46 countries, including the U.S. under both Trump administrations, affirming a commitment to hardline opposition to abortion and promoting the heteronormative nuclear family “as foundational to society.” Critics have noted that many of the agreement’s signatories are led by notoriously authoritarian governments with harsh restrictions on LGBTQ+ people. For example, Saudi Arabia’s maximum penalty for gay sex is death , and Russia classifies the “international LGBT movement” as an extremist group. During his first week in office, former president Joe Biden withdrew the U.S. from the GCD just months after its launch, stating , “It is the policy of my Administration to support women’s and girls’ sexual and reproductive health and rights in the United States, as well as globally.” But Huber, now out of her government job and leading the anti-abortion NGO Institute for Women’s Health (IWH), continued to champion the agreement. She’s traveled around the world meeting heads of state, including in Burundi and Argentina , who would quickly go on to join the GCD, while developing more concrete plans to carry out its goals. IWH did not respond to a request for comment. Within the first week of Trump’s second term, the U.S. rejoined the agreement, and in June, the U.S. assumed the leading secretariat position among its signatories. Via says pushing the core group initiative while the U.S. is the secretariat is likely strategic timing. “The U.N. is seen as the boogeyman for far-right and Christian Nationalist groups, because their definition of human rights is expansive and inclusive, which is not what these organizations want,” Via says. “But they’re gonna work within the system because it looks like they have an opportunity.” Huber has advocated in favor of the core group since August and has said that the GCD is “the substantive basis” for the work ahead. “What has not yet been built is the intentional, sustained coordination that turns a shared commitment into shared strategy at the international negotiating table,” she told The Washington Stand. “A nation that arrives at a negotiation alone is outmatched. A nation that arrives having strategized with 40 others is not.” The who’s who of the far right are on board Faith leaders praying over Donald Trump in March 2025. Image via The White House . Fair use . The September 17th forum was held in the hopes of creating a roadmap to execute the plans for the core group. The event was sponsored by Well Versed, an evangelical NGO whose mission is to bring “biblical principles of governance to government leaders and the people who elect them.” The forum attracted a number of noteworthy guests. There were three representatives from the Trump administration, including Deputy Secretary of State Christopher Landau, Director of HHS Global Affairs Bethany Kozma, and Ellie Cohanim, the senior policy advisor at the U.S. mission to the U.N. Leaders from several U.S.-based right-wing organizations also made appearances , including Turning Point USA Faith , C-Fam — which holds special consultative status at the U.N. — and Salt and Light Council , a group focused on getting churches involved in right-wing politics. Via called these groups “the usual suspects” when it comes to work like this, but noted that their power has grown in recent years. In addition to the power players from the U.S., there was a stacked lineup of folks from the global right. Lawmakers from Peru, Uruguay, and Guatemala, all countries where CIVF has been active, were present. Also in attendance was Artur Pawlowski, a Canadian far-right pastor known for his role in the Alberta Separatist movement; Armenian evangelical activist and former politician Stepan Sargsyan; and Dutch lobbyist Henk Jan van Schothorst. What this lineup indicates, Via says, is that the Christian far-right is interested in wielding its outsized influence in the Trump administration to impact the global stage. “It is the traction that the Christian nationalists have gained since Trump has been in office,” she says. “Because of the administration’s willingness to wield power and influence in other countries based on this Biblical worldview … you have had some political leaders be more accepting of the idea.” What could this mean? In her interview for The Washington Stand, Huber said that the point of the core group is to organize concrete action towards the goals of the GCD, which on its own is a non-binding agreement with no mechanism to enforce or ensure compliance among its signatories. One way the core group should achieve that, Huber says, is through Protego, a project launched in 2023 by IWH that creates a road map for countries to follow in their policymaking on issues of women’s health. Outlined in their Women’s Optimal Health Framework , IWH advocates against abortion and promotes sex education that prioritizes abstinence and “prepar[ing] for a healthy marriage and future family.” While the 62-page guide makes no explicit mention of LGBTQ people, Sjödin says that this kind of sex education, which has been widely criticized as ineffective , “is focused on promoting heterosexuality as the only form of acceptable sexuality.” “It is used to push these binary norms that are harmful for anyone who doesn’t live up to it or doesn’t agree with it, and it limits access to education for young people who need to know both about themselves, especially if they don’t think of themselves as heterosexual, but also about everyone else so that they have an understanding that humans are different.” Giammattei speaking at an IWH conference in 2021. Screenshot via the Government of Guatemala YouTube . A few countries have already adopted Protego’s framework. Guatemala was the first , establishing a partnership with Huber and the IWH in June 2023 under the leadership of far-right then-president Alejandro Giammattei. The Protego project worked with the country’s Ministries of Health, Education and Social Development and developed a “Parent Child Communication Guide” that would promote IWH’s narratives on sex and family planning to Guatemalans. Huber claims the guide, which was spread throughout the country via partnerships with influencers and faith and business leaders, has reached 3 million school-aged children in Guatemala. Huber and Ugandan First Lady Janet Museveni signing the agreement of their partnership on Protego in 2024. Screenshot via UBC Television Uganda YouTube . Uganda, where gay sex is punishable by death , was the next country to adopt the framework in early 2024. Unlike in Guatemala, specific details have been difficult to access and not publicly shared, but promoting abstinence-only sex education has been a publicly stated priority. Other countries, including Hungary and Burundi , have also signaled their support for Protego, but less is known about their actions on the matter. What happens now? While the new core group has not yet been officially established, statements by Lara and Huber suggest an intention to do so in the near future. “[It will take] less time than people assume, because the hardest part is already done,” Huber said in her Washington Stand interview. “The coalition exists. The shared commitments are on paper and have held through changes of government in multiple countries.” Ipas, in its briefing, emphasizes that there is still a way to go before the core group’s establishment and cautions advocates to “avoid overstating [its] legitimacy and power.” However, Sjödin warns that the plans, and the danger they present, must be taken seriously. “Currently, we are seeing quite an extensive and horrendous backlash against LGBTQ+ people,” she says. “What they potentially want to do here is to actually make inclusion of everyone more difficult.” Written by Uncloseted Media

title: How an extremist network articulated a hoax linking Brazil’s President Lula to child abuse on X
description: Distortion in the meaning of a speech by Lula about prostate cancer exams went viral within hours and fed conspiracy theories amid a tight presidential race in Brazil.
content: Monitoring of 1,819 posts showed far-right users tried to manipulate Grok, X’s AI tool Originally published on Global Voices Brazilian President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva. Art by: Méuri Elle/Aos Fatos , used with permission. This article was originally published on the fact-checking agency Aos Fatos website , on September 30, 2026. It is part of the joint initiative Laboratório de Investigação Eleitoral (Investigative Electoral Lab) with Agência Pública , Amado Mundo and Núcleo Jornalismo . An edited version is republished here under a partnership agreement between Global Voices and Pública. A few days before the first round of the 2026 general elections in Brazil on October 4, it took only a few hours for a line said by President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva about preventive exams for prostate cancer to be twisted into a pedophilia accusation against him . Aos Fatos obtained and checked 1,819 posts on X (formerly Twitter), which reconstructed how this hoax was planted and harvested by Bolsonarista users on social media between September 28 and 29. The distortion in the meaning of Lula’s speech stemmed from a false pedophilia accusation that had already been boosted hours ahead of a statement he made at a campaign event in the city of Belém, Pará state, on September 28. Users manipulated questions asked to Grok , X’s AI assistance tool, to make it state “Lula consumes CP” — an acronym in English for child pornography. The chatbot warned that the sentence was wordplay and that it had no records to support the claim. However, the edit cut from Lula’s speech, shared on social media, gave the narrative new momentum. Besides requests to make the video viral and to mobilize influencers, some publications also revived old episodes and characters without any connection to Lula’s line to back theories associating the president with child abuse. During his rally, Lula was talking about the importance of cancer prevention and criticizing men’s resistance to having prostate exams, compared to women’s healthcare culture, which, according to him, is used to having gynecological exams from an early age. The beginning Among the publications with broader reach identified by the survey, one of the first to cut a quote from Lula’s speech was posted at 11.59 p.m. on September 28 by Pâm, an influencer, founder of a Bolsonarista site called The Incorrupt, and member of Estúdio 5, a pro-Bolsonaro content-making hub aligned with Catholicism. A user identified as Pâm posted: ‘Lula saying women ‘learn to be touched ever since they are little’ WHAT THE FUCK, PRESIDENT? Are you NUTS???.’ Image : Screenshot from X. Fair use. At 12.28 a.m. on September 29, the Space Liberdade account published another cut from the same quote. It took only a minute for the interpretation to be turned into an explicit accusation. At 12.29 a.m., two other posts were already calling the president “a pedophile”; one of them requesting users to pass this claim along. In the following hours, several users started acting to amplify the reach of the accusation. Posts asked people to download and repost the video, suggested boosting the hashtag #LULAPEDOPHILE, and included messages like “it has to go viral.” At 2.48 a.m., a profile proposed to pick out two sentences from Lula’s speech, create a hashtag, and mobilize 10 to 20 influencers around it. An account called Space Liberdade posted: ‘URGENT — Lula says men don’t like ‘to be touched’ and states that women learn ‘to be touched’ since they are little. (…) a man doesn’t; he doesn’t know that once he has prostate cancer they will touch him a lot.’ Image: Screenshot from X. Fair use. Five hours before Pâm’s publication, users connected to the so-called “bolha da resenha” (hangout banter bubble) were already experimenting with Grok, forcing the tool to associate Lula with pedophilia. The term describes an ecosystem of profiles, most of them anonymous, that combine aggressive humour, extremist political content, and reproducing chans aesthetics — anonymous forums well known as one of the main cradles of the current far-right. One of the first users started with the words “cerveja e picanha” (beer and filet steak) and asked the tool to summarize the expression with its initials in two letters, manipulating it to write “Lula consumes CP” (child pornography). After that, other profiles set new instructions and made the chatbot create similar sentences. The stories crossed paths overnight. At 3.39 a.m., a user shared a cut with the line about “touch” and asked Grok if Lula was “addicted to CP.” At 4.10 a.m., another one reloaded the association in a comment on Space Liberdade’s post. The survey also found references to codes like “Jack” and “CPzeiro,” besides slogans such as “PROTECT OUR CHILDREN” and “LULA DON’T TOUCH OUR CHILDREN.” Overall, 43 percent of the posts analyzed (746) had straightforward pedophilia accusations or, besides accusing Lula, encouraged the propagation of this assumption. Poster widely shared on social media featuring a girl and the message: ‘Lula, leave our children at peace!’ Image: Screenshot from X. Fair use. The narrative was already formed by the time it reached profiles with major political prominence. At 9.49 a.m. on September 29, Nikolas Ferreira , a die-hard Jair Bolsonaro ally and member of the Chamber of Deputies, published one of the cuts. At 10.23 a.m., he shared a video playing Lula’s quote and saying: “A little girl doesn’t learn to be touched in any way, Lula!!!” Ferreira had been linked to the “hangout banter bubble” before. In September 2025, after the killing of conservative US activist Charlie Kirk , members of the group celebrated Ferreira’s posts saying he had “joined the hangout.” At the time, the politician published a version of the Pepe the Frog meme , a channer mascot, featuring his own image and saying “Be the far-right that they fear.” The survey doesn’t indicate that the Congressman had taken part in these recent experiments with Grok or in creating the accusation against Lula. Yet he shows up among the first politicians with a wider reach to boost the narrative, hours after it started circulating. A while after Ferreira’s posts, expressions associated with this narrative were among X’s trending topics. “PROTECT THE CHILDREN,” which was ranked 28th at 9.04 a.m., jumped to the first spot by 11.15 a.m. At the same time, “LULA DON’T TOUCH THE CHILDREN” was in fourth, and “pedophile” in 20th. On September 30, the Superior Electoral Court (TSE) gave Nikolas Ferreira a 24-hour deadline to remove his post on X. Minister Estela Aranha argued that he had attributed an “entirely different connotation” to the original quote, taking it out of the public health context and associating it with crimes. From misinformation to conspiracy After it went viral, the hoax no longer relied on what was said in Belém. Social media accounts started to revive episodes and characters without any connection to it to introduce Lula as a member of an alleged pedophile network or ring. These theories also reached Telegram and WhatsApp groups monitored by Aos Fatos. Besides claiming Lula had defended or “trivialized” pedophilia in his speech, messages started to talk about a “likely inclination to pedophilia” and to introduce isolated episodes as an indication of such behaviour. One of the allegations exploited the fact that the speech took place in the state of Pará, where several cases of sexual violence against children had allegedly occurred in the local Marajó archipelago . “A geographical and discursive coincidence that should, at least, cause embarrassment rather than applause,” read one of the messages. There is no evidence linking Lula to such crimes registered in the region. Sexual violence against children and teens is a real and documented problem, but it has also been a target of false and unsubstantiated allegations for years. Some of the posts included statements made in 2022 by Senator Damares Alves, then minister of women, family, and human rights in Bolsonaro’s cabinet, saying she had been attacked for denouncing abuses in Marajó Island. At the time, Alves said she had received testimonies about children who had had their teeth removed to facilitate oral sex and were forced to ingest pasty food to facilitate anal sex. The allegations weren’t registered by any investigative bodies, and the Federal Prosecution Office (MPF) presented a public civil action against Alves for spreading what they classified as “sensationalist false information involving sexual abuse and torture to the children of Marajó.” Some posts also started to associate Lula with Jeffrey Epstein , the disgraced US financier accused of leading a network of sexual exploitation involving minors. What was used as evidence for that was an email attributed to Epstein in which he claims to have talked to Lula on the phone, during the time Lula was imprisoned in Curitiba, Brazil, through Noam Chomsky. The email exists, but it doesn’t prove whether the conversation ever occurred . Valeria Chomsky, Noam’s wife, denied he had mediated it. When the email was first publicized, the Social Communications Office of the Presidency said that “the referred phone call never happened.” This kind of phone call would also be incompatible with the rules of the Federal Police prison ward where Lula was held, according to experts interviewed by Folha de S. Paulo newspaper . Other Brazilian politicians were also mentioned by Epstein , including former president Jair Bolsonaro, whom the financier referred to once as “the man.” Written (Português) by Pública – Agência de jornalismo investigativo Translated (English) by Fernanda Canofre View original post (Português)

title: Hong Kong police launch AI-powered national security platform for school pupils
description: The tech allows students to generate personalized stories on China’s “holistic approach to national security” – a framework advocated by President Xi Jinping covering areas from politics and economy to ecology and technology.
content: ‘May the seeds of national security take root and sprout in the hearts of the pupils…’ Originally published on Global Voices Hong Kong police launch an AI-powered national security education platform for the city’s pupils during a ceremony on October 6, 2026. Photo: HKPF, via Facebook. Used with permission. This article was originally published by Hong Kong Free Press on October 13, 2026. The following version is republished on Global Voices under a content partnership agreement. It is also part of Global Voices’ October 2026 Spotlight series, “ Big Tech and Authoritarianism .” You can support this coverage by donating here . Hong Kong police have launched an artificial intelligence-powered national security education platform for young students. The NSmarties AI Interactive Platform was officially launched on October 6, 2026, at a ceremony at Precious Blood Primary School in Ap Lei Chau, with about 700 pupils attending, police said in a Facebook post : 【 NSmarties童心護港AI互動平台 • 正式啟動 】 國家安全，由童心出發！ 由警務處國家安全處主辦的「NSmarties童心護港AI互動平台」今日（6日）於海怡寶血小學正式啟動！ 警務處處長周一鳴、警務處副處長（國家安全）江學禮、寶血會總會長區綺雯修女等一眾嘉賓，聯同約700位同學一同見證這個重要時刻。 啟動禮圓滿結束，標誌着國安教育以創新科技走進校園的新里程！ 願國安種子在同學心裏生根發芽，茁壯成長！ [ NSmarties: Children’s Hearts Protect Hong Kong AI Interactive Platform • Officially Launched ] National security begins with the hearts of children! Organized by the National Security Department of the Hong Kong Police Force, the ‘NSmarties: Children’s Hearts Protect Hong Kong AI Interactive Platform’ was officially launched today (6th) at Sea View Precious Blood Primary School! Distinguished guests, including Commissioner of Police Joe Chow Yat-ming, Deputy Commissioner of Police (National Security) Kelvin Kong Hok-lai, and Sister Au Yee-man, President of the Precious Blood Society, joined some 700 pupils in witnessing this momentous occasion. The successful launch ceremony marks a new milestone in bringing national security education into schools through innovative technology! May the seeds of national security take root and sprout in the hearts of the pupils, and grow strong! The platform, jointly developed by police and Hong Kong Qianfan Technology, lets students generate personalized stories centered on China’s “holistic approach to national security” — a framework pushed by Chinese President Xi Jinping that covers areas from politics and the economy to ecology and technology. It also features the voices of Chow and security chief Chris Tang, who explain the city’s national security laws and security information. The ceremony marked a “milestone” in bringing national security education into the city’s schools through innovative technologies, police said. The NSmarties platform was first unveiled on National Security Education Day in April, but it was not fully launched to the public at that time. Hong Kong has strengthened national security education alongside a crackdown since Beijing imposed a national security law in 2020 following the 2019 protests and unrest. Beijing inserted national security legislation directly into Hong Kong’s mini-constitution in June 2020 following a year of pro-democracy protests and unrest. It criminalized subversion, secession, collusion with foreign forces and terrorist acts — broadly defined to include disruption to transport and other infrastructure. The move gave police sweeping new powers and led to hundreds of arrests amid new legal precedents , while dozens of civil society groups disappeared . The authorities say it restored stability and peace to the city, rejecting criticism from trade partners , the UN and NGOs . Written by Hong Kong Free Press

title: Peru’s Indigenous people in Cutivireni and Oviri take the front line against Amazon wildfires
description: As El Niño worsens dry conditions, Peru’s indigenous people in Cutivireni and Oviri are taking action to protect their Amazon territory from wildfires.
content: Indigenous guardians play a critical role in protecting the land, their homes, and their livelihoods Originally published on Global Voices The Cool Earth initiative in Cutivireni and Oviri works around three key concepts: the monitoring of satellite fire weather alerts, the introduction of a flag-based system regarding safe times to conduct traditional fire practices, and practical training to contain small blazes and prevent them from causing devastation to the Indigenous people in the rainforest. Photo by Cool Earth, 2026; used with permission. It’s September and 2026 has already been defined by wildfires spanning across the globe. Driven by the heat and dryness of the climate crisis, outbursts on the edge of Bordeaux, France have forced 200,000 from their homes and led to deaths in Spain . Smoke has billowed across the Canada-U.S. border, covering cities in smog. Fires are expected to continue as seasons transition in the Southern Hemisphere, with a severe El Niño phenomenon that the United Nations warns will add pressure to an already scorching globe, risking similar conditions to those that — back in 2024 — drove the worst Amazonian wildfires in two decades . With fire and drought risks set to increase in the coming months, Indigenous people in the Amazon rainforest are stepping up to take on new roles as fire brigade members, protecting both their homes and a key natural resource in the fight against climate change. Ahead of this year’s El Niño weather pattern, Indigenous people from Peru’s Cutivireni and Oviri communities approached Cool Earth: they wanted to ensure they were equipped to fight any fires this coming season. The organization’s long-established relationship with the two Indigenous groups and experience working with the Central Asháninka of the Ene River to create the Paamari programme , made it easier to establish four fire crews across communities that were already springing into action. In Cutivireni, the newly formed Chullachaqui fire crew have faced multiple blazes. Named after an Amazonian forest spirit , the crew understand the critical role they play in protecting the land, their homes, and their livelihoods. In early August came one of the first tests of their training: alerted by people in the Tsyapo and Pajonal communities, community brigade members joined up with their partners in Central Cutivireni to tackle the fire, which they successfully put out. Julio Acosta, Cool Earth’s Forest Data Manager, said that the organization really admires and appreciates how the communities have been making the best use of what they have been building with them, adding, “This early action taken in Tsyapo and Pajonal demonstrates how effectively they put into practice what they’ve learned in the workshops.” The training was taken directly from concepts in the Paamari programme . Similar to Paamari, the Cool Earth initiative with Cutivireni and Oviri works around three key concepts: the increased monitoring of satellite fire weather alerts, the introduction of a flag-based system regarding safe times to conduct traditional fire practices, and practical training to contain small blazes and prevent them from causing devastation to the Indigenous people in the rainforest. The communities themselves often act as the brigade’s eyes, alerting them to smoke or flames. Working in close coordination with local authorities, brigade members first assess the wildfires and try to tame the blazes in their initial stage, before they require a more complex response by the authorities. Acosta stressed the importance of highlighting the fact that the main work of these brigades lies in prevention, rather than initial response. “This tends to be less visible,” he explained, {but the measures they take, such as the flag system, help reduce the occurrence of these fires. Seeing the initiative and eagerness to learn more from the brigade members motivates us to expand and improve the work we’ve been implementing together.” Along with protecting their homes, the Indigenous communities act as custodians of the rainforest — a vital global asset for fighting the climate crisis. According to the World Resources Institute, rainforests provide 23 percent of the climate mitigation needed to help stabilise global temperatures. Their destruction from wildfires depletes the world’s natural carbon stores and also releases tons of carbon back into the atmosphere. At the moment, not every fire can be tackled. August saw a fire in Cutivireni that reached a score of three out of five on Peru’s national disaster response . When interviewed, onlookers noted that there was “little that’s left or [that] survived.” The fire raged for four days and went on to destroy 50 hectares of land – about the size 70 football pitches. With communities set to come under more strain, Cool Earth hopes to establish further training, turning the initiative into a fully fledged project. Providing Indigenous people with more finance and training capabilities, they hope to meet the ever-growing demand for wildfire training in the Peruvian Amazon. Written by Cool Earth

title: How authoritarian states are building an international market for digital surveillance
description: Digital authoritarianism is not developing in isolation, but through the international exchange of technologies, standards, and practices.
content: The main danger of AI in authoritarian regimes is the ability to suppress any protest Originally published on Global Voices Moscow subway cameras are connected to a facial recognition system. Screenshot taken from the YouTube video “Facial recognition cameras help detain dissidents in the Moscow metro” by the DW YouTube channel ; fair use. This post is part of Global Voices’ October 2026 Spotlight series, “ Big Tech and Authoritarianism .” In this Spotlight, we explore how Big Tech facilitates and hinders authoritarian governments and practices, and how these choices influence the Global South. You can support this coverage by donating here . Sonya, from Stavropol Krai, Russia, is 15 years old. In June 2026, she was sentenced to 70 hours of compulsory labor, connected to a February 2026 incident in which she had written the surname “Navalny” on a bus stop . That stop happened to be in a district that was being monitored by officers from the Center for Combating Extremism , commonly called Center E. Similarly, Yuri, a pensioner from Astrakhan who was also identified from surveillance footage, was given three years of restricted freedom for writing “No to War” in red marker on buildings. Authoritarian regimes are increasingly using artificial intelligence (AI) as a technology of political survival. Cameras with facial recognition, video analytics, biometric databases, digital IDs, social media monitoring, Deep Packet Inspection (DPI) systems, and public service platforms are gradually merging into a single infrastructure of control. Such a system makes it possible not only to observe citizens in real time, but also to reconstruct their past movements, connections, habits, communications, and political activity. The main risk is that AI and related technologies make repression faster and less visible: the state no longer needs to constantly demonstrate force if citizens know they can be identified retroactively. Modern digital authoritarianism is not developing in isolation, but through the international exchange of technologies, standards, and practices. China , Russia , Iran, Belarus, Venezuela, countries in Africa, Western and Central Asia, and companies connected to them, sell and exchange AI infrastructure tools that are being used for the purpose of repression. Western technologies a re also being bought and exchanged within authoritarian regimes. Large language models In early June 2026, Sberbank Deputy Chairman Alexander Vedyakhin told Reuters that the company was offering countries in the Global South access to Russian AI models that would take “local values” into account. Vedyakhin was referring to specific large language models (LLMs) — GigaChat and YandexGPT — which Russia had been trying to develop since 2019. However, as IT expert Alexander Isavnin told journalists at the podcast Zhivoy Gvozd, Russian generative AI models lag behind American and Chinese models and cannot even generate text in Cyrillic . Yet, new national and sovereign AI models are supposed to reflect traditional values, including patriotism , service to the Fatherland and responsibility for its fate, a strong family, historical memory and continuity between generations, and unity of the peoples of Russia. These models are expected to be trained on domestic, authentically Russian material. It is reasonable to assume that in countries like those in Western Asia, Russian AI models will reflect adherence to Islamic traditions, while in Argentina, perhaps, they will reflect respect for football from an early age. Developers, meanwhile, do not understand how people with no idea about how any of this works can write AI laws: “In places, the document reads as if it was written by people who had only ever seen LLMs in local news.” From the perspective of global democracy, however, this illiteracy among Russian lawmakers suggests that Russia is unlikely to supply LLMs to autocracies around the world. China, by contrast — unlike American developers — makes its language models open in principle, meaning that anyone can take the code and modify it for their own needs. In China, all LLMs are controlled and tightly regulated by the state, so party censorship is written into the code from the start — for example, you cannot get an answer about the Tiananmen Square protests. However, the models are distributed as open source, which is why more than 50 percent of Chinese model users come from developers, including those in the Global South. At the same time, the U.S.-based ChatGPT can easily replicate AI-generated Iranian propaganda videos, in which the main characters are Lego figures. Only once, a France 24 investigation showed, did the chatbot alert the journalist that he might be inadvertently reproducing propaganda, but desisted when he said it was only satire. Mass surveillance systems AI also includes other tech developments, like the so-called “smart city” systems which, in the Chinese version, imply comprehensive surveillance of a state’s own citizens. This can include video surveillance, wiretapping, internet censorship, facial recognition systems, ethnic profiling, and so on. In supplying such systems to the Global South, China has overtaken Russia. Yet, Russia is not lagging behind in the use of AI to surveil its own citizens. State media write that Moscow has long moved beyond the threshold implied by the concept of a “smart city.” Today, it includes a complex digital urban ecosystem made up of video surveillance, AI, big data, and the “internet of things.” According to estimates by Comparitech , two of the ten cities outside China with the highest number of cameras per person are Russian: Moscow and St. Petersburg. The list also includes four Indian cities, Seoul in South Korea, Baghdad in Iraq, Kabul in Afghanistan, and Singapore. In China itself, the number of cameras has practically reached a ratio of one camera for every two people: the largest mass-surveillance system in the world. Russia has sold , and in some cases, continues to supply its surveillance software products to other authoritarian states, while remaining technologically dependent on China. In 2024, up to 80 percent of all cameras used in Russia were made in China and sold under Russian brands. China has built one of the most sophisticated domestic systems of digital control; it has also turned the export of digital infrastructure into part of its foreign policy via the Digital Silk Road , launched back in 2017. Through the initiative, China promotes digital infrastructure, technological cooperation, standards, and solutions for countries in Asia, Africa, and Latin America. Formally, these projects are described as support for the digital transformation of developing states, but they deepen partners’ dependence on Chinese technologies and create channels for the spread of AI systems, especially mass-surveillance technologies. Experts from the Carnegie Endowment , the European Parliament , and Freedom House agree that the main danger of AI in authoritarian regimes is the ability to suppress any protest before it has even properly materialized. AI systems can help authorities detect early signals: unusual online activity, preparations, movement patterns, and links between activists. All of this has, among other things, already been done in the digital Gulag that Moscow has built. As journalist Andrei Zakharov writes in his new book “Russian Cyberpunk,” Moscow authorities have been collecting comprehensive data on Muscovites since as early as 2014, and have been using AI to bring information from different agencies into a single database. After the 2021 protests, activists were arrested using facial recognition systems. According to Zakharov, in Moscow in 2023, there were already more than 220,000 video devices connected to a unified data storage and processing center. Now, against the backdrop of sentences of ten-plus years for publishing an article in a foreign journal, for example, the sentences handed down in 2021 to people prosecuted after the so-called “ Palace Case ” seem small — but this was the first instance in which people in Russia were arrested as a result of video surveillance analysis. Police came to Yevgeny Yesenov’s apartment and arrested him the day after the rally ; he became the first prisoner in the case and was sentenced to four years in a penal colony, though he was released on parole after a year and a half. While things like this happened in pre-war Russia, now, as a result of organized surveillance by the “smart city” system, anyone’s address can be found using their face. After the start of the full-scale invasion of Ukraine, people were arrested in the same way for anti-war graffiti or for setting fire to military enlistment offices — any forms of protest that had been captured and analyzed by the country’s AI surveillance system. As T-Invariant writes , Russia is also developing AI for drones and cryptography at Moscow State University under the leadership of Putin’s daughter, using Chinese and American gray-market chips and open Western AI technologies . It is also sharing such technologies with China and North Korea. China and Western Asia Chinese participation in “smart city” projects in Western Asia is unfolding in a region where, according to the EIU Democracy Index for 2023 , 16 out of 20 territories are classified as authoritarian regimes. These projects are most highly concentrated in the Gulf states: the UAE has 11 projects, while Saudi Arabia has seven. Outside this bloc, Turkey plays the most visible role with five projects, while the remaining projects are distributed among Algeria, Egypt, Iraq, Iran, Morocco, and Tunisia. The latest Chinese concept of the “smart city,” from 2022, involves real-time information monitoring across virtually all aspects of urban life. This technology makes it possible to establish continuous real-time digital monitoring of a city, giving the government the ability to multiply its control over citizens. China and Russia’s links with Iran In February 2026, research by the civil society organization Article 19 found that the architecture of internet control in Iran relies heavily on Chinese technologies. The report said that China supplied Iran with facial recognition technologies, internet filtering equipment, and surveillance tools from companies such as Huawei, ZTE, Hikvision, Tiandy, as well as smaller Chinese suppliers. At the same time, an investigation by Le Monde and Forbidden Stories showed that Iran acquired the Russian facial recognition system FindFace , developed by NtechLab, through Iranian intermediary companies. The software was resold to entities linked to the Iranian state, including the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) and the Ministry of Intelligence. As early as 2019, when Iranian women began receiving fines by mail for not wearing the hijab while in a car, citizens have been talking about their government’s use of digital surveillance. In December 2025, Iran and Russia signed a cooperation agreement in the fields of AI, cybersecurity, the digital economy, blockchain, fintech, and partnerships with the private sector. Surveillance of people in authoritarian regimes is organized by both cameras and control of internet traffic. The Russian company Protei , headquartered in Jordan but rooted in St. Petersburg, has reportedly supported Iran’s efforts to introduce systems for interception, monitoring, and traffic management, as well as to integrate DPI into network architecture. Its clients include MTN Irancell, Iran’s largest telecom provider, as well as operators and government entities in Tajikistan, Uzbekistan, Pakistan, Kenya, Namibia, Qatar, and other countries. Taraneh M., an artist living in Iran who was detained during the “Woman, Life, Freedom” protests , said that in 2022 she had prepared for the possibility of arrest by securing her devices, deleting confidential information, and setting self-destruct timers for personal chats. Nevertheless, investigators presented her with a thick dossier of her social media posts, some of which dated back five years. Although she has been released, Taraneh is now afraid to speak on the phone lest she is being monitored. The China-Russia relationship Although AI development in China has surpassed Russia’s, cooperation exists in the supply of Chinese technologies, as well as scientific development. In January 2025, on the heels of Russia’s attempts to create a network of AI alliances with BRICS and other non-Western partners, Vladimir Putin instructed the Russian government and Sberbank to deepen cooperation with China, especially with regard to AI “technological research and development.” The immediate stimulus was sanctions, Russia’s access to advanced chips and AI equipment was restricted after its invasion of Ukraine, but its dependence on China has persisted in recent years. Supplies for new servers, for example, which Russia does not manufacture, came from China through intermediary firms. As T-Invariant discovered , however, joint developments are being conducted in two areas: training AI for drones and mass surveillance of people. In November 2025 , the creation of two joint laboratories was announced: one for nano-structured optoelectronic materials and devices, and another for AI algorithms and their applications. North Korea gets involved Russia and North Korea are cooperating in testing AI in military operations : North Korea supplies weapons that are tested in Russia’s war on Ukraine , and data that may improve North Korean systems, including AI-guided systems, is passed back to North Korea. In May 2026, North Korea tested high-precision cruise missiles and artillery systems with AI guidance. According to analysts, “AI” likely refers to automatic target recognition and terminal-stage guidance, although the level of technological sophistication remains unclear. Since late 2023 , North Korea has supplied Russia with ballistic missiles and artillery rockets, and their use on the battlefield in Ukraine is believed to have given Pyongyang, and likely Russia, valuable operational data. The China-Venezuela-Belarus triangle In Venezuela, authoritarian digital control is being built through international supply chains. Regimes do not necessarily create such systems themselves. Instead, they buy cameras, servers, video analytics platforms, DPI systems, algorithms, and software, often from countries also experiencing digital authoritarianism. China’s Dahua , despite being added to the U.S. Entity List in 2019 because of its involvement in repression in Xinjiang, retained access to the Venezuelan market and discussed the integration of AI into surveillance systems with the authorities. Possible participation by Huawei , ZTE , and China CAMC in projects is also mentioned, although their role remains unspecified. Between 2021 and 2023, the Venezuelan interior ministry also held talks with the Belarusian company Synesis , which is under U.S. sanctions for technologies that Belarusian authorities used to identify and arrest protesters. The Kipod software offered to Venezuela included facial recognition; searches for specific people and routes; license plate recognition; detection of weapons, abandoned objects, smoke, and crowds; perimeter control; and monitoring of traffic violations. Countries on the African continent A 2026 Institute of Development Studies (IDS) report on surveillance in “smart cities” in Africa showed the spread of Chinese AI-surveillance systems in 11 countries, including Algeria, Egypt, Kenya, Rwanda, Senegal, and Zimbabwe. Carnegie’s study on the global use of AI in human surveillance predicted that the adoption of such technologies in Africa is likely to grow. Chinese exports of surveillance systems are being used in authoritarian contexts — including in Uganda and Myanmar, often through companies such as Huawei, Hikvision , and Dahua. As in Western Asia, China-Africa cooperation in AI may look like assistance in developing “smart cities,” but its repressive use is connected with control over citizens. Central Asia included Governments in Central Asia have actively purchased Chinese digital public-security systems. A report by the Caspian Policy Center says that in 2013, Tajikistan cooperated with Huawei to create a safe city surveillance system in Dushanbe worth about 22 million USD, largely financed by a Chinese loan. Other publications note that Chinese companies occupy leading positions in “safe” and “smart city” projects across Eurasia, especially because the region offers relatively open markets for Chinese technologies. Chinese censorship systems and related tools have also appeared in Kazakhstan, Pakistan, and Ethiopia, but cooperation between China and Central Asia mainly represents the export of AI surveillance technologies under the rhetoric of crime prevention. What can be done? Even supposedly democratic states have employed surveillance technologies to spy on their citizens. One of the most functional proposals to hinder the development of such authoritarian digital tools is to make Western technologies open source, and move digital strategies away from sovereignty and towards inclusion of the majority world : not as territories of extraction for the energy and water to run powerful data centers that serving Western AI models, but as actual participants in digital strategies and AI governance. Such an approach would include sustainable development and practical concerns like agriculture, healthcare, education, transport, urban planning, adaptation to climate change, and many more human-centered priorities. Written by Daria Dergacheva

title: Norway’s Telenor telecom faces lawsuit for giving user data to Myanmar junta
description: "We hope this will finally lead to accountability for the harms Telenor has caused Myanmar people through its conduct and its dangerous divestment."
content: The state-owned company is accused of abetting crimes against humanity Originally published on Global Voices Telenor telecom operated in Myanmar from 2014 to 2022. Photo by Bjoertvedt. Source: Wikipedia. CC BY-SA 4.0 This post is part of Global Voices’ October 2026 Spotlight series, “ Big Tech and Authoritarianism .” In this Spotlight, we explore how Big Tech facilitates and hinders authoritarian governments and practices, and how these choices influence the Global South. You can support this coverage by donating here . The Norway-based multinational telecom company Telenor is facing charges for its role in turning over sensitive customer data to the military government of Myanmar. If successful, the case would be the first ever to hold a telecom company accountable for failing to protect user data from being misused by an authoritarian regime. Telenor operated in Myanmar from 2014 to 2022 with 18 million subscribers. After the February 2021 coup , Telenor faced pressure after the junta demanded compliance with its surveillance and content blocking directives. Telenor decided to leave Myanmar, but civil society groups raised strong objections that its local operations would be sold to a company with links to the junta. In December 2024, activist group Justice For Myanmar filed a complaint against Telenor in Norway for breach of the Sanctions Act. Norway rejected it, but the complaint was refiled in October 2025 with an additional charge of aiding and abetting crimes against humanity. The Norwegian state has a 54-percent stake in Telenor. In December 2025, the Norwegian Parliament initiated an investigation into the operations of Telenor in Myanmar. The leader of the disciplinary committee of the Parliament said: “We must uncover how a state-owned company could cooperate with a brutal military regime (by handing over) customer information about the opposition [in Myanmar].” In April 2026, a civil class action lawsuit was filed against Telenor in Norway by Myanmar citizens for sharing their sensitive personal data with the junta. The complaint alleged that Telenor shared at least 1,253 phone numbers with the regime. The data also included call logs and location data, names, addresses, ID numbers, Facebook, and bank accounts linked to mobile numbers. Among the complainants is Tha Zin, the widow of rapper and lawmaker Phyo Zeya Thaw , who was arrested based on a trumped-up charge, convicted, and later executed by the junta. Tha Zin said her husband was arrested right after his account information was accessed by the junta. I lost my husband. It is not just a wife losing her husband. It is also a loss to the movement. It is also a loss to democracy because my husband was committed to democracy and a youth leader. Losing him means a loss to the country. Lawyer Jan Magne Langseth summed up the content of the complaint. Telenor ASA in Norway clearly contributed to the practice of handing over user data, despite the inherent risks for its customers in Myanmar. We have evidence of cases where the team at HQ expressly recommended the data to be handed over. In September 2026, Norway’s National Criminal Investigation Service and the interior security service searched the office of Telenor related to the charges filed against the company. Justice for Myanmar spokesperson Yadanar Maung welcomed the decision of Norway authorities to investigate Telenor. Telenor’s transfer of spyware to a military-linked company and sharing of sensitive data with the military junta was extensively documented We hope this will finally lead to accountability for the harms Telenor has caused Myanmar people through its conduct and its dangerous divestment. In several statements sent to the media, Telenor said it is cooperating with authorities with regard to the ongoing investigation. It added that it needed to defend its employees in Myanmar. In Myanmar, refusing requests from the military authorities could, in the worst case, have led to imprisonment, torture or the death penalty. Telenor Myanmar had no real options. We could not play Russian roulette with the lives of our employees. Telenor media relations director David Fidjeland reiterated the same point. Our employees risked imprisonment, torture or the death penalty if the military authorities’ orders were not complied with. We found that we had no real choice and that we could not put our employees’ lives at risk. Telenor acknowledged the brutality of the junta, but it asserted that the welfare of its employees should not be endangered. Telenor acknowledges that human rights due diligence must consider all rights-holders. However, when faced with the brutal force of the military, Telenor maintains that an employer cannot give instructions that put employees’ lives at direct risk. Civil society groups said the investigation is a step forward in fighting impunity . Civicus said companies should not enable human rights abuses. The Telenor case has the potential to challenge impunity. It should refocus the minds of democratic states and companies headquartered in them, offering a warning that they can be exposed for complicity in the junta’s atrocities. It should give fresh impetus to civil society’s efforts to hold states and companies to account. Faiz Naeem, Asia Pacific policy analyst at Access Now, added that Telenor’s case is a reminder for companies that their obligation to users does not end when leaving a country under an autocratic regime. The decision to investigate Telenor for crimes against humanity should be a wake-up call for every technology and telecom company operating in a high-risk environment: leaving a market does not mean leaving your human rights responsibilities behind. The civil class action lawsuit is seeking damages of EUR 9,000 (roughly USD 10,500) per customer. Written by Mong Palatino

title: In Kyrgyzstan, persons with disabilities are collecting proof of physical barriers to hold the government accountable
description: Lived experience can reveal things that a conventional audit may miss.
content: Physical barriers are being exposed by those who are affected the most Originally published on Global Voices Participants of the Oasis Data Lab workshop in Bishkek, Kyrgyzstan. Image by the public fund Oasis. Used with permission. This interview is part of a series of spotlights on the work of some of the grantees of the Digital Spark granting scheme, as part of the Regional Support Mechanism EECA project, implemented by the Metamorphosis Foundation and TechSoup , in partnership with CIVICUS and under the Digital Democracy Initiative (DDI) that covers the Global South. It is being published on Global Voices as part of a content-sharing agreement. Kyrgyzstan’s progress in creating an inclusive and accessible environment for people with disabilities remains limited after seven years of ratifying the United Nations (UN) Convention on the Rights of Persons with Disabilities in 2019. Despite a legal responsibility to undertake measures that would remove legal and physical barriers and help people with disabilities lead independent social and economic lives, the government has not prioritized this commitment at the level requested by the country’s disabled community. In such circumstances, holding the government accountable requires proof of how much physical infrastructure remains inaccessible for the more than 218,000 people with disabilities in the country — about three percent of the population. One of the organizations leading this effort in Kyrgyzstan is the public fund “Oasis” , which is documenting the level of physical inaccessibility in the capital, Bishkek, with the help of people with disabilities who are auditing objects through their real-life experiences. Global Voices conducted a written interview with Oasis to learn about this work, which is being carried out under the Digital Sparks project. The interview has been edited for clarity and brevity. Global Voices (GV): Please tell us about your organization and why you chose to get involved with the Digital Sparks project. Oasis (O): Founded in 2003, Oasis is a Kyrgyz civil society organization working to build inclusive communities where everyone can participate and reach their full potential. We joined the project because we know that it is not possible to build an inclusive city without listening to the people navigating its barriers every day. In Bishkek, we saw accessibility discussed through policies and assumptions, while lived experiences remained largely invisible. We wanted to change that to make exclusion visible, measurable, and impossible to overlook with the help of data. Digital Sparks helped us build the Oasis Data Lab, bringing together citizen-generated data, digital mapping, storytelling, and advocacy. Our goal was not simply to create a map, but to build a bridge between lived experience and public decision-making, turning everyday barriers into evidence for change. GV: What issue/challenge in your community prompted you to undertake this project? O: The project grew from a practical problem: people with disabilities face barriers across Bishkek, but these barriers were not being systematically documented. Public transport, entrances, ramps, toilets, signage, and other parts of the urban environment can make everyday participation difficult. Yet without reliable and regularly updated data, these problems remain easy to overlook. Kyrgyzstan ratified the UN Convention on the Rights of Persons with Disabilities in 2019, but there is still a gap between formal commitments and everyday accessibility. Previous assessments were limited and did not create a living public record that could be used to monitor progress. We therefore started from a simple principle: before accessibility can be improved, it has to be measured. And the people who experience these barriers every day should be directly involved in producing that evidence. GV: What are the key changes/activities that your organization implemented during your participation in the project? O: Through Digital Sparks, we developed Oasis Data Lab into a more structured space for digital civic participation. We brought together more than 30 young people, including people with physical disabilities, blind and low-vision participants, deaf participants, social activists, and urban experts. We organized workshops on disability rights, inclusivity, digital advocacy, data collection, mapping, and storytelling. A major practical change was integrating UrbanEyes into our work. Through the application, participants can assess buildings using geolocation, photographs, questionnaires, and standardized accessibility indicators. The web platform then visualizes this information through an interactive map, filters, heat maps, and accessibility indices. Most importantly, the project moved us from collecting individual complaints toward creating structured, comparable civic data that can support advocacy, dialogue with authorities, and evidence-based urban planning. GV: How did your participation in the project impact your organization’s beneficiaries and the community that you serve? Please provide examples. O: One of the biggest impacts has been the shift in how participants are positioned: not simply as beneficiaries, but as researchers, digital monitors, and civic actors. Participants have already assessed 350 buildings across Bishkek and transformed their observations into geo-referenced data for the city’s accessibility map. The results show the scale of the problem clearly: 60.3 percent of assessed buildings had a ramp-related barrier, either because there was no ramp or because the existing ramp was difficult or unsuitable to use. The project also allows participants to compare accessibility across districts and types of buildings, rather than relying only on individual complaints. Just as importantly, participants are learning to communicate findings through digital storytelling and advocacy. Their lived experience is becoming structured evidence that can be presented directly to decision-makers and used to argue for concrete improvements. GV: How has your own knowledge, awareness, and experience with digital democracy and civic space changed, thanks to your participation in the project? O: The project changed our understanding of digital democracy. We previously saw digital tools mainly as instruments for research, communication, and advocacy. Digital Sparks helped us understand their deeper democratic potential: digital democracy can change not only how information is shared, but who gets to produce it, whose voices are visible, and who participates in decision-making. Participatory mapping showed that technology can shift evidence production closer to communities themselves. People can document the barriers they experience, make them visible, and use this evidence to demand change. We also learned that digital democracy must be accessible, safe, and rights-based. More importantly, we realized that as society becomes increasingly digital, traditional forms of participation alone are no longer enough. Digital democracy offers an opportunity to make civic participation more inclusive, responsive, and effective. GV: What are the most valuable lessons and experiences you are taking away from this project? O: Our most valuable lesson is that “Nothing About Us Without Us” should apply not only to policymaking, but also to the evidence on which policy is based. Lived experience can reveal things that a conventional audit may miss. A checklist may show that a building has a ramp, while a wheelchair user can show that the ramp is too steep, slippery, too narrow, lacks handrails, or still does not allow independent access. We also learned that data must remain dynamic. Accessibility cannot be measured once and considered solved; information needs to be updated and connected to advocacy. Finally, data alone does not create change. Its value comes from combining reliable evidence with storytelling, community leadership, public communication, and structured dialogue with institutions. That combination is what turns information into civic power. GV: What comes next? How will you apply the learning and digital capacity you have built in your future work and within your community? O: Our next step is to make Oasis Data Lab a long-term civic innovation and evidence hub rather than a one-time project. We plan to continue developing the UrbanEyes app and Bishkek’s Accessibility Map , regularly updating the data and using it to identify priority areas and support public accountability. We also intend to use the findings in dialogue with Bishkek’s Mayor’s Office, the Ministry of Labour, Social Protection and Migration, civil society, businesses, and other stakeholders. The data can help identify areas requiring urgent improvement and support more informed infrastructure planning and budgeting. Participants will be encouraged to continue contributing data, producing digital stories, and sharing their skills with other young advocates. In the longer term, we want to adapt this model to other regions, especially rural ones. Written by Nurbek Bekmurzaev

title: What telecoms leave behind when they exit a country
description: “While the network will continue to provide service to users, the transparency practices and internal procedures and protocols for data safeguards may change after a sale.”
content: When telecoms pull out of markets, data protection and human rights commitments often disappear Originally published on Global Voices Image by Akil Mazumder via Pexels . Used under a Pexels license . By Jie Zhang This post is part of Global Voices’ October 2026 Spotlight series, “ Big Tech and Authoritarianism .” In this Spotlight, we explore how Big Tech facilitates and hinders authoritarian governments and practices, and how these choices influence the Global South. You can support this coverage by donating here . In March 2022, just over a year after Myanmar’s military coup, Telenor, the Norwegian telecommunications giant, sold its subsidiary in the country to M1 Group, bringing nearly eight years of operation to an end. But leaving Myanmar did not end the controversy surrounding its departure. Instead, the hasty exit came back to haunt the company over the next four years. Since then, criticisms, lawsuits and litigation by civil society and affected people have continued to follow the company. The scrutiny also reached a crescendo this September, when Norwegian authorities opened criminal investigations into Telenor over allegations of aiding crimes against humanity in the country and transferring sanctioned surveillance equipment during the sale. Within days, a court in Norway also green-lit a class-action lawsuit brought on behalf of a group of Telenor’s former customers in Myanmar. Telenor reiterated its position upon the investigation, arguing that any alternatives would have endangered the employees’ lives. Yet the company’s trouble raises a broader question that many telecommunication multinationals may have to confront one day: When a company decides to exit a “high-risk market,” where does its responsibility end? Leaving is not just a business decision Under military rule, Telenor faced government demands to facilitate surveillance, hand over the personal data of dissidents and activists, and restrict access to information. In a market like this, staying may cease to be viable. For a telecom operator, the matter is not simply to make a choice between remaining in the market or leaving, but whether it can exit in a way that minimizes further harm to users, without leaving them more vulnerable. Unfortunately, Telenor failed to do so. In a conventional asset sale involving multinational companies, the transaction may center largely around physical and commercial assets, such as factories, equipment, and inventory. Selling a telecom subsidiary is another story. As gatekeepers of internet access and digital information, telcos control sensitive user data, including location records and device logs. They also serve as key intermediaries for interception systems and have the technical capacity to cut off network access. In a sale, the company hands over not just infrastructure and commercial assets, but also systems and data that can expose the movements and footprints of millions of users. Without rigorous buyer scrutiny and assessments of the risks associated with the transfer, a corporate sale may lead to grave harm to users, who might be watched, tracked, or even silenced in authoritarian contexts. What followed in Myanmar showed that the risk was anything but hypothetical. It also revealed why powerful companies cannot simply shed their responsibilities by selling their business, when people depending on their services are left to bear the consequences. A global pull back is underway This matters because Telenor’s withdrawal from Myanmar is hardly an isolated case. After the debacle, the telecom giant began systematically pulling back from its Asian markets. In 2022, the company combined its Malaysian subsidiary Digi with local telecom service Celcom. In Thailand the following year, it merged its local business dtac with True Corporation before later selling down most of its stake in the entity. It also completed its sale of Telenor Pakistan to PTCL at the end of 2025, with further plans to dispense with its remaining Asian assets. Zooming out, multinational telecom operators are shrinking the overseas footprints they spent decades building. MTN, Africa’s largest telecom operator, announced its plan to “ orderly exit ” from the Middle East in 2020 amid geopolitical risks. The company has ended its operations in Syria , Yemen , and Afghanistan by 2025. MTN also completed the sale of its operations in Guinea-Bissau and Guinea-Conakry in 2024, citing unsustainable costs. Aiming to refocus on a small group of more profitable core markets — Britain, Brazil, Germany, and Spain — Spanish telecom giant Telefónica also accelerated its retreat from Spanish-speaking Latin America. In 2025 alone, it sold its subsidiaries in Argentina , Peru , Uruguay, and Ecuador , followed by exits from Colombia , Chile , and Mexico in early 2026. The reasons for telecoms’ departure vary from geopolitical tensions to high costs. However, we should ask the critical question: what changes for the customers after a telecom operator leaves them behind? What gets lost in the handover While the network will continue to provide service to users, the transparency practices and internal procedures and protocols for data safeguards may change after a sale. This is where the risks of market exit are less visible. Telenor, MTN, and Telefónica have all developed sophisticated governance systems, including formal human rights policies, data-protection and security procedures, and regular transparency reporting. Research shows they are among the strongest performers on transparency and accountability in the telecom industry. Those transparency reports provide a useful window into how telcos handle government demands. The reports describe the procedures in place to respond to government requests for user data, content restrictions, and network disruptions, and publish data on such requests across different markets. Although transparency alone cannot prevent abuse, it creates a public record of how governments exert pressure on companies. However, we found that transparency reporting mostly does not survive ownership changes. Once a multinational operator leaves a market, it naturally stops reporting in that country. Disappointingly, its successors overwhelmingly fail to maintain the same level of transparency. Millicom, a recurring buyer of Telefónica’s Latin American assets, acquired its operations in Uruguay and Ecuador, and a controlling stake in Colombia. Millicom does publish law-enforcement disclosures, but the data are aggregated by region rather than by country. Moreover, as of September 2026, only the 2024 report is publicly available. Elsewhere, the picture is even bleaker: None of the other recent buyers appeared to publish transparency reports or commit to continuing their predecessors’ transparency practices. The discontinuation of transparency reporting removes the opportunity for the public to scrutinize whether or not the volume of the government demands changed after each ownership transition. It also hides from view how those demands are handled internally. Transparency reporting, however, is only the tip of the iceberg. Beneath it lies a much broader mechanism of user data protections, institutional norms, and governance safeguards, such as risk escalation channels, legal and human rights checks, and many more. In authoritarian states, multinational telcos are no less likely to face government pressure to shut down networks, block websites, or hand over user data. While these companies may also have limited room to resist, they usually operate under more institutional oversight than state-controlled ones. They are also exposed to more scrutiny from the international press and civil society, greater reputational risk, and often stronger regulatory frameworks established by their home countries. By contrast, many operators who succeeded these businesses might be more closely connected to governments and more deeply embedded in the local political and regulatory environment. Facing fewer external constraints from society, media, and NGOs, they also have less willingness and fewer resources to challenge governments. What a more responsible exit might look like Since safeguards may weaken or even disappear with ownership shift, the essential duty to protect users’ rights should not be treated as an afterthought to a market exit. It must be a key element of the transaction. For telecom companies, a responsible exit should begin well before a buyer is even selected. Before entering Myanmar in 2014, Telenor commissioned a human rights impact assessment (HRIA) for its planned market entry. The company also states that it considered human rights and data privacy as it prepared for its departure. But there is no public record showing that Telenor conducted a standalone assessment of the human rights risks of the exit itself. Companies should commission a mandated, exit-specific human rights impact assessment, evaluating what user risks the sale itself might create, the concerns of stakeholders and users, how the data might be used or transferred in the future, and which groups of users would be most exposed to the risks it identifies. Buyer due diligence should go beyond financial stability to examine the buyer’s human rights record, its capacity to govern sensitive data, and whether existing safeguards can survive under new ownership. Moreover, a responsible exit from any politically risky market should also ask a basic question: What should not be transferred in a sale? Should every piece of user data be handed over to the next owner? Telecom companies should evaluate if any sensitive data can be segregated, anonymized, or even deleted whenever feasible, particularly when transferring such data could expose high-risk users. Similarly, some technical infrastructure, such as surveillance equipment, interception systems, and other network-control capabilities, should not be bundled into a sale automatically as ordinary infrastructure. Norwegian authorities are now probing whether Telenor transferred sanctioned surveillance equipment as part of the sale of Telenor Myanmar without the required authorization from the Norwegian government. A new test for the next exit If Telenor offers a lesson for everyone about what can go wrong in a reckless departure from a high-risk market, MTN’s unfinished exit from Iran may offer a test about whether companies can approach their next departure differently. MTN still holds a 49 percent stake in Irancell. The current U.S. sanctions on Iran also complicate any attempt to exit. Earlier this year, MTN also protested after the CEO of Irancell was ousted by the Iranian authorities over delaying an internet blackout order during the domestic protest. This arguably makes MTN’s position in Iran even more difficult than Telenor’s trajectory in Myanmar. When MTN is finally able to withdraw from the country, can it exit in a more responsible way? Written by Ranking Digital Rights

title: Independent journalism under siege in Georgia
description: Georgia’s deteriorating press freedom is part of a broader process of democratic backsliding, with the right to peaceful protest severely restricted, opposition politicians jailed, a decline in judicial independence, and more.
content: Need for a unity became urgent in April 2025, after the law on approval of foreign grants Originally published on Global Voices Photo by Slava Taukachou on Unsplash This article by Elli Kostika is an edited version of a longer piece , first published on June 11, 2026, by the non-profit journalism organization Incubator for Media Education and Development (iMEdD) . This excerpt is published on Global Voices, with permission under a CC BY-NC 4.0 license. Any use of images or charts by third parties requires permission. As Georgia has dropped to 135th place in the 2026 World Press Freedom Index, iMEdD spoke with representatives of four independent media outlets about the challenges facing journalism in the country: imprisonments, attacks, “foreign agent” laws, and the struggle for survival. Tamar Rukhadze, Deputy Director of Georgian outlets Batumelebi and Netgazeti , describing the state of Georgia’s press, said: Ι cannot remember any other period in Georgia’s recent history, since I’ve started as a journalist in 1997, with such a harsh and hostile environment towards journalists, media workers and civil society. Georgia’s government, led by the Georgian Dream party, has intensified its crackdown on media by adopting a series of restrictive laws aimed at suppressing the country’s independent media. Meanwhile, Georgian journalists have been facing constant threats , from legal challenges to physical attacks. Georgia’s deteriorating press freedom is part of a broader process of democratic backsliding , with the right to peaceful protest severely restricted , opposition politicians jailed , a decline in judicial independence, and a disputed election in October 2024 . Although Georgia has been an EU candidate country since 2023 , the ruling Georgian Dream Party, founded by oligarch Bidzina Ivanishvili, has pivoted the country’s foreign policy towards Russia . However, large segments of Georgia’s population remain pro-EU, and citizens have been protesting for over 500 consecutive days since November 2024, following the contested October 2024 elections and the government’s decision to suspend efforts to advance Georgia’s EU accession process until 2028 . As the struggles of Georgia’s independent journalists have intensified in this increasingly repressive environment, so too has their determination to survive. A CEO behind bars, yet her colleagues press on Batumelebi and Netgazeti have paid a heavy price for their independence. The outlets’ co-founder and CEO, Mzia Amaglobeli, was arrested on January 12, 2025, after an altercation with a police chief in Batumi, Georgia’s second-largest city. Following a trial which press freedom groups denounced as politically motivated, Amaglobeli has been sentenced to two years in prison . In December 2025, the European Parliament awarded her the Sakharov Prize for Freedom of Thought . She remains detained under deplorable conditions. Her eyesight — already poor before her imprisonment — is now almost completely lost, Rukhadze tells us, while her lawyers spent six months securing permission for her to visit a clinic, as medical facilities within the penitentiary system lack proper equipment. In an interview with iMEdD, Rukhadze stresses the deep psychological effects Amaglobeli’s sentence has had on the newsrooms. “ We aren’t the same as we were earlier before this imprisonment,” adding, “It’s a nightmare for every single journalist to become news.” Rather than resorting to self-censorship, Batumelebi’s and Netgazeti’s journalists have persisted in their reporting. She highlights: The first thing Mzia did after her arrest was to send a message from prison, asking her team to continue their work as before — to do what they had always done and what they are known for: professional, ethical watchdog journalism that gives a voice to those who need it most. Weaponizing the law Arrests and detainments are only one of the ways the Georgian government uses legislation against the country’s independent media.
