Nino Bakradze, co-founder and editor-in-chief of iFact , tells iMEdD they have lost 90 percent of their income since May 2025 owing to a series of laws that have restricted the outlet’s access to foreign funding. Georgian media, civil society organizations, and individuals receiving financial support from abroad are obligated to register as foreign agents under the 2025 Foreign Agents Registration Act (FARA) and face criminal liability for noncompliance. When such provisions are combined with the 2025 amendments to the law on grants , which require foreign donors to obtain governmental approval before offering grants to Georgian recipients, the causes for iFact’s financial troubles become clear. Because foreign grants had been a major source of funding for Georgia’s online media for years, as Rukhadze explains, iFact’s financial situation is far from unique. Batumelebi and Netgazeti are also struggling financially: “It’s not about a bright future or expansion or professional growth or anything. It’s about just survival,” Rukhadze stresses. In March 2026, access to foreign funding was further restricted when the Georgian parliament adopted new amendments to the law on grants , expanding the definition of a “grant.” In 2023, the ruling Georgian Dream government tried to adopt legislation requiring media and civil society organizations that receive over 20 percent of their funding from abroad to register as “foreign agents.” Although mass protests prevented its immediate adoption , the “Law on Transparency of Foreign Influence,” commonly known as the “Russian law” due to its perceived similarity to Russia’s “foreign agent” law, was passed in May 2024 . Batumelebi and Netgazeti have refused to register as foreign agents, Rukhadze tells us, as have most Georgian independent media. Amid such restricted legal and political circumstances, the trust between sources and journalists has been disrupted. Georgians are now often reluctant to talk to iFact’s journalists and request to speak under anonymity in fear of consequences, explains Bakradze. There have been cases of people who have lost their jobs or access to social aid after openly criticizing the government, she adds. Attacks, smear campaigns, and surveillance Since 2023, watchdogs have recorded 65 cases of physical assault and 83 verbal attacks against Georgian reporters . Sulkhan Meskhidze, who started working as a journalist in 2010, is no stranger to physical and verbal harassment. Such incidents have intensified in the last five years, he tells iMEdD, highlighting that in nearly half of his in-the-field reporting trips, he becomes the target of attacks. The most serious attack Meskhidze faced came in February 2025, while he was reporting on the deaths of two kids at a public construction site in an area of Batumi called “Dream City.” A group of people began throwing stones at him and demanding that he leave. According to Meskhidze, the aggressors were local residents and government supporters. The police were present, Meskhidze says, but did nothing to protect him. Even when he managed to record and publish evidence of such attacks, authorities still remained indifferent. iFact has recently experienced a different type of attack, in the form of smear campaigns. After the outlet published an investigation regarding how Russian oil continues to move through Georgian ports despite international sanctions, the European Commission decided to put Georgia’s Kulevi port on a potential sanctions list. Following that, in March 2026, pro-government media “labeled us as spies of the British intelligence service,” Bakradze explains. Physical and digital surveillance presents another challenge for iFact. “A lot of the time we see the state security people around us,” Bakradze says. Their phones are also being surveilled and cyberattacks are common. Survival tactics: From wine tasting to yoga Bakradze, who co-founded iFact in 2016, tells iMEdD she would not have decided to establish an outlet today. When you start the week on Monday, you never know if you’ll last until Friday or not. Since losing their foreign grant revenue, iFact is now relying entirely on local Georgian-derived income, selling a monthly newsletter on sanctions evasion, while also offering a paid membership , the first outlet in Georgia to do so, she says. Events are another revenue source, with iFact organizing a wine tasting event in May 2026. What has helped iFact’s reporters cope with stress is making themselves busy and seeing the results of their investigations, Bakradze says, adding that “we do yoga as a team.” Sulkhan Meskhidze worries mostly about the stress his family is facing, who live in constant fear for his wellbeing. “The lights must stay on” Georgia’s independent media have forged a collective response in the form of Sinatle Media , a solidarity and sustainability network of 22 online media. As Sinatle’s Chair of the Board and journalist at the investigative outlet Studio Monitor , Teo Kavtaradze tells iMEdD, the need for a united front became increasingly urgent in April 2025, after the law requiring government approval to obtain foreign grants was adopted. Following a lengthy bureaucratic process, Sinatle Media was born in July 2025. The Georgian journalists who spoke to iMEdD all work for media outlets that belong to the network. In Georgian, Sinatle means “light.” Both the name and the network’s slogan, “The lights must stay on,” were chosen to underscore a shared conviction: “If the lights go out, the truth disappears with them,” Kavtaradze highlights. One of Sinatle Media’s main functions involves collecting funds that are allocated to its 22 members. Through a series of events, including book fairs, flea markets, and artwork auctions, Sinatle has managed to raise GEL 260,000 (approximately EUR 84,000). The network also provides cost-sharing services, which proved particularly valuable in December 2025 during a smear campaign against the network. Sinatle Media helped its members secure legal support to counter these allegations. One of Sinatle’s main achievements, according to Kavtaradze, is that this is “the first case when we [Georgian media] are actually helping each other […] and we are building this solidarity together.” Written by GV Contributor

title: Riddims against copyright
description: Dancehall’s interactive, collaborative nature doesn’t treat a work as isolated or even something that is “finished.” Iteration is a part of the creative process that is decided by the next function or party.
content: The Caribbean has long been exploited on the world stage, and copyright law is no exception Originally published on Global Voices Copyright chaser from eff.org . Fair use. By Alexis Hancock “Oh! Bob Marley, right?” Jamaican culture has been popularised by the mainstream, and as a Jamaican-American, I often get a glimpse into how others have consumed it and from what point of view. I would not call myself an ardent Marley fan, but I know the kind of people who are most likely attached to his music outside of Jamaica — for example, the potential counterculture student of the 1970s at UCLA who found connection to his messages of resistance. My personal fascination with Jamaican music is the “riddim” — the Jamaican patois spelling of “rhythm” — an instrumental beat or tune constructed not for a single artist, but to be used by the collective of the time and to be both enjoyed and critiqued by the culture makers of Jamaican art: the disenfranchised masses. As a public interest technologist and digital rights advocate, I view the “riddim” with an open-source lens. It helped to protect Jamaican culture, particularly from Western constructs that are heavily embedded in existing power dynamics like rigid copyright laws and the corporate commodification of music. Riddims Dancehall’s interactive, collaborative nature doesn’t treat a work as isolated or even something that is “finished.” Iteration is a part of the creative process that is decided by the next function or party. In Larisa Kingston Mann’s “ Rude Citizenship ,” she outlines how copyright law was written at a time when many of the island’s people were themselves considered property under slavery, thereby creating — from the very start — a contentious relationship with those holding the society’s wealth. Copyright law was set up for those with ample resources to dictate what could be protected and who could profit. Beat-sharing directly challenges neo-colonial copyright’s individualistic definition of ownership and originality. Traditional copyright promotes monopoly over expression , enforced by harsh legal mechanisms (such as statutory damages ) that make intertextuality, reuse, and artistic experimentation legally risky. Even Sean Paul, one of the most commercially successful dancehall artists in the world, attributed his mainstream success of “Get Busy” to the Diwali Riddim . If not for this collective creativity and shared use, we would not see dancehall music evolve and get pushed to the world in the way that it has. Collective sharing didn’t stop at just music; dance was often learned collectively as well. I used to watch “ passa passa ” videos in high school and college, just to learn and keep up to date with the latest dances coming out of Jamaica and New York City in the early 2000s. These parties were the bane of anyone entrenched in respectability. The clothes were outlandish, the manners “rude,” the dancehall queens nothing short of acrobatic, and the parties could go until 6:00 a.m. But this was also the time when new artists could get a slot, vendors could make a little money, and producers could collaborate with artists and get public consensus on what worked before dropping money at a studio. Caribbean economics Library of Congress – Banana farming in Jamaica. Fair use. The Caribbean has long been exploited on the world stage in many ways, and copyright law is no exception. Jamaica was often sidelined into less than favourable international trade agreements that didn’t keep the interests of the Jamaican masses in mind. More often than not, there was a strict one-size-fits-all structure, dictated by the International Monetary Fund (IMF) and the World Bank: detrimental loan structures, one-sided economic trade agreements, currency devaluation, and exploitative labour guidelines. In 1992, the IMF created terms that heavily impacted Jamaica’s economy. This served as the backdrop for the Jamaica Copyright Act of 1993, when the country was directed to reshape its laws to participate in global trade. More rigid terms forced artists to start registering “riddims,” and while these laws are purported to protect artists, less resourced and independent artists struggled to make claims against large producers. This also killed the “handshake agreements” many artists and producers made prior to 1993. Modern dancehall and beyond A dancehall party flyer. Photo courtesy of OpenVerse . Public Domain. This hasn’t stopped dancehall creators from organising alternative circuits of commerce and performance, social intimacy, and communal engagement. Even today, the continuous nature of dancehall works still causes friction with how copyright laws function. This year, a monumental copyright case was overturned by a U.S. federal judge who named many famous artists in a list of 150, and affected about 2,000 tracks. The plaintiffs, Cleveland “Clevie” Browne and the heirs of Wycliffe “Steely” Johnson , claimed that the “Fish Market” riddim (also known as the “Pocoman Jam riddim”) was the basis and source of the percussion pattern that runs through reggaeton , the now billion-dollar musical genre with origins in the Spanish reggae of Panama brought by Afro-Jamaican migrants, and further magnified by Puerto Rican artists. However, the logic was denied . As US District Judge André Birotte Jr. said, “Plaintiffs have not clearly identified what copyrighted work contains the allegedly protectable selection and arrangement they seek to enforce.” The claim failed to take all selections and arrangements mentioned and tie them to one work. But rather, it referenced a collection of works that mirrored parts over time: “That principle is especially significant here. Skidmore cautioned that a plaintiff cannot ‘reconstitut[e] the copyrighted work as a combination of unprotectable elements’ and then claim that those elements are substantially similar because they appear in an accused work, even where the elements are presented in ‘a different aesthetic context.’” The nature of riddims is a double-edged sword here. Browne and Johnson were deprived of a chance to share in the profits of their creativity that set the groundwork for a whole new genre of music. If this lawsuit had gone in their favour, the logic could potentially have put any new reggaeton artist to this profit-sharing standard, possibly resulting in conditions only well-backed artists like Bad Bunny could afford to accommodate. Such an outcome could have created a disempowering dynamic for new artists. A power structure riddims fought in the first place. We can all easily hear the main percussion in Puerto Rican reggaeton and Dominican dembow, but copyright’s ears are selectively biased against rhythm — usually favouring money, the artist’s will to attribute credit to where it’s due, and when the tracks were created in the more popular artist’s career. In fact, Black artists are often credited much later for genre-defining work and after lighter-skinned artists have made their money. Despite the mainstream push away from collective processes, dancehall continues to evolve. What “makes Jamaicans cool” is the layers of understanding that come with what we share. Copyright creates a stamp in time — a piece of “the cool” the mainstream can manage to freeze and sell. Yet, the true cool develops alongside the collective and remains protected by that shared understanding. Written by Global Voices Caribbean

title: Venezuela faces a deepening energy crisis as protests grow
description: Venezuela’s worsening electricity crisis is disrupting daily life, pushing frustrated residents into the streets as prolonged blackouts expose the fragility of the country’s power grid.
content: For most of the population, unreliable electricity has become a chronic part of daily life Originally published on Global Voices Screenshots of protests in four states in Venezuela (Zulia, Lara, Portuguesa and Falcón) amidst power cuts across the country, taken from the YouTube video by NTN4 “Venezuelans can’t endure power cuts anymore and take to the streets in protest,” published on September, 3, 2026. Fair use. This piece is part of Global Voices’ September 2026 Spotlight series, “ Protest in Democracy .” With this Spotlight, we seek to explore the many forms of protest, the tactics states use to delegitimize and suppress them, and the complex relationship between protest and democracy. You can support this coverage by donating here . “Yesterday we didn't have electricity for 11 hours. The day before, it was seven,” explains Yanira, a 33-year-old artist and designer who lives with her ailing 73-year-old father in Maracaibo , one of the cities most affected by Venezuela’s electricity rationing. In a region where temperatures remain high throughout much of the year, going without electricity is more than an inconvenience. For her family, the blackouts directly affect their health , work and daily routines. And Yanira is not alone. Across the country, increasingly long and unpredictable blackouts are disrupting work, education, businesses and sleep. In several cities, frustration has spilled into the streets, with residents protesting outages and blocking roads in the darkness. In August, residents of various cities, including Turmero and Valencia, took to the streets at night to protest the worsening situation. Their demonstrations came as authorities expanded electricity rationing in response to growing pressure on the country’s fragile power grid. The crisis is particularly severe outside Caracas, where scheduled outages lasting between six and 15 hours a day have been reported in several regions. Authorities have also introduced shorter working hours for some public sector employees, and reached an agreement with shopping malls to reduce electricity consumption. The government has attributed the worsening shortages in part to the effects of El Niño , which has brought drought and unusually high temperatures to Venezuela. There is also, however, a series of factors worsening the situation, like the major failure at Guri Hydroelectric plant , where one of its turbines — which generated 770MW — collapsed. The country’s electricity problems long predate the current weather conditions. Venezuela’s power system has suffered from years of underinvestment , poor maintenance and allegations of corruption , resulting in a system that is increasingly unable to meet the country’s electricity needs. A crisis measured in lost hours For residents of Maracaibo , one of Venezuela’s largest and most economically important cities, the crisis has become deeply personal. Yanira says she can spend at least six hours a day without electricity. The outages have affected both her livelihood and her mental health. She has had a hard time finding a job or even working remotely, because blackouts make it difficult to function. She eventually began running small businesses from home, first selling sandwiches and cepillados zulianos — shaved-ice treats popular in the region — but keeping food frozen and drinks cold is a constant challenge when electricity can disappear without warning: View this post on Instagram The hardest moments come at night. Without air conditioning, sleeping becomes difficult in Maracaibo’s intense heat — and while opening the windows brings some relief, it also lets tropical insects inside. Yanira says the situation has affected her sleep so severely that she began taking sleeping pills. Her experience reflects a broader problem. According to Venezuela’s 2025 Living Conditions Survey, only around 10 percent of Venezuelans live without experiencing power outages . For most of the population, unreliable electricity has become a chronic part of daily life. The blackouts are also taking a toll on local economies. The National Chamber of Commerce reported that 38 percent of businesses had closed during the year, amid the combined effects of the electricity crisis and the country’s broader economic difficulties. In Puertos de Altagracia which, like Maracaibo, is situated in Zulia state, Sara Hernández works at a company that sells bottled drinking water. Even with access to a generator, keeping the business running during outages is difficult because fuel is not always available. The uncertainty makes planning almost impossible. Electricity can disappear at any moment, and some businesses experience more than one rationing period in a single day. The consequences extend beyond commerce. In Maracay, in Venezuela’s central region, resident Kellys Gallardo told El País that she receives daily text messages from the state electricity company, Corpoelec, warning her about planned outages, but the messages sometimes arrive only after the power has been cut. Gallardo, who works at a company that manufactures printer ink cartridges, experiences outages both at work and at home. Her children are also affected when electricity rationing disrupts their schools. From frustration to protest As blackouts grow longer and less predictable, anger is becoming increasingly visible in public spaces. Residents who once endured outages quietly are now gathering in the streets, blocking roads and demanding solutions. In cities like Turmero, Valencia, El Tocuyo , Caja Seca , Calabozo , Zaraza and Valle de la Pascua , nighttime protests have highlighted how deeply the electricity crisis has entered everyday life. The year 2026 saw a significant surge in both the frequency and widespread nature of civil unrest across Venezuela. The Observatorio Venezolano de Conflictividad Social (OVCS) documented upwards of 4,000 protests between January and August , a figure that OVCS coordinator Marco Antonio Ponce noted is triple the amount seen in earlier comparable timeframes. Daily demonstrations averaged 22 in August alone, with persistent electricity blackouts ranking among the public’s primary grievances. For Venezuelans, the problem is about more than having to sit in the dark. It means businesses losing products and working hours, children having no electricity at school, families struggling to sleep in extreme heat, workers unable to plan their days, and people unable to access healthcare. In the Barquisimeto dialisis unit, for example, a lack of power left 42 kidney patients without treatment . A problem that has lasted for years Venezuela’s current electricity emergency echoes its 2019 crisis, when severe drought reduced water levels at the Guri reservoir, the hydroelectric complex that supplies a major share of the country’s electricity. One the most important events of this period was a 6six-day national blackout. Today’s crisis is unfolding on top of years of deterioration in the electricity system. Venezuela has an installed generation capacity of approximately 30,000 megawatts, but currently produces less than half of that amount. The gap becomes particularly problematic during periods of high demand. The government recently announced new investments aimed at rebuilding the system. In June, authorities signed an agreement with U.S.-based General Electric to restore 1,000MW of generating capacity over two years, with plans for an additional 5,000MW over the following four years. Another agreement involving the Tocoma hydroelectric project, which began construction in 2007 but was never completed, was also announced. Authorities say these projects form part of a broader effort to recover Venezuela’s electricity infrastructure. For residents living through the outages, however, long-term plans offer little immediate relief. In a country where electricity shortages have persisted for years, each new blackout carries the weight of a much longer story: one in which an essential public service has become increasingly unreliable, while residents are left waiting for the lights to come back on. Written by Gabriela Mesones Rojo

title: In Bosnia and Herzegovina, children with Down syndrome are using a video game to safely navigate the internet
description: Being able to use the internet safely is also about being able to participate in everyday life.
content: A virtual assistant called Sol the Owl guides kids through the game Originally published on Global Voices SafeClick is a video game that teaches children with Down syndrome about digital safety. A virtual assistant, Sol the Owl, that guides them through the game. Image by the game's developers, used with permission. This interview is part of a series of spotlights on the work of some of the grantees of the Digital Spark granting scheme, as part of the Regional Support Mechanism EECA project, implemented by the Metamorphosis Foundation and TechSoup , in partnership with CIVICUS and under the Digital Democracy Initiative (DDI) that covers the Global South. It is being published on Global Voices as part of a content-sharing agreement. Like their peers, children and young people with Down syndrome are curious about technology and the internet, but there are often no suitable, dedicated tools to help them learn how to safely navigate the web. This is true in Bosnia and Herzegovina as well, where children with cognitive disabilities are underserved and tend to end up in digital isolation because of caregivers’ concerns about digital safety and the risks of being online. There are approximately 550-700 children and adolescents with Down syndrome in the country. They are supported by three specialized associations nationwide: the Association “Life with Down Syndrome of FBiH ”, Down Syndrome Association Mostar , and DOWN SY I MI . To teach online safety, these organizations have to rely on online safety tools that heavily feature text, abstract explanations, and complex language, which are not accessible or meaningful for children with Down syndrome. Stefan Filipovic. Photo used with permission. A group of developers, IT professionals, and designers in Bosnia and Herzegovina has been working to address the lack of a digital safety tool tailored to children and adolescents with Down syndrome. Their goal is to help young people understand, practice, and feel confident making decisions online. Global Voices conducted a written interview over email with Stefan Filipovic, a member of this group, to learn how they created a video game to teach children with the genetic condition about digital safety. The interview has been edited for clarity and brevity. Global Voices (GV): Please tell us about your organization and why you chose to get involved with the Digital Sparks project. Stefan Filipovic (SF): We are a group of IT professionals, developers, and designers from Bosnia and Herzegovina. Most of our work is in commercial technology, but we also have experience developing educational and socially useful video games, such as Eureka – Edukativna videoigra , an educational game for children, and Lea & Leo , a game about children with diabetes. We joined the Digital Sparks project because we wanted to use that experience for a group that, in our opinion, is often overlooked when digital products are designed. Young people with intellectual disabilities are using phones and the internet, but many digital tools are simply not designed with their needs in mind. The video game SafeClick ( Siguran klik ) allowed us to work on something practical and useful while also learning how to design more inclusively and to involve educators and users in the process. GV: What issue/challenge in your community prompted you to undertake this project? SF: While working with Servis Centar “Dajte nam šansu – Zvjezdice” – an association and day center that provides free support to children, young people, and people with developmental disabilities, we saw that young people with Down syndrome were using phones and the internet, but there were very few cyber-safety resources made specifically for them. Most materials use a lot of text, complicated explanations, or interfaces that are difficult to follow. To our knowledge, parents and educators often end up focusing on limiting internet use rather than teaching young people how to deal with unsafe situations. We wanted to try something different. With SafeClick, we use simple stories, familiar situations, pictures, and game mechanics to help users practice what to do when they receive a suspicious message, meet someone online, or experience cyberbullying. GV: What are the key changes/activities that your organization implemented during your participation in the project? SF: We developed the first playable version of SafeClick. The game is currently awaiting approval by the App Store and Google Play. It is designed for mobile devices, with simple, accessible interactions and visual scenarios. One important decision was to avoid punishing users for mistakes. Instead, the game explains what happened and gives them another chance. We worked closely with educators and parents and used their feedback to make the scenarios easier to understand. We are currently in the phase of arranging mentoring sessions with the mentor assigned to us through the project, with the aim of earning additional opportunities to promote the game and reach as many users as possible. GV: How did your participation in the project impact your organization’s beneficiaries and the community that you serve? Please provide examples. SF: Although the game will be published soon, the initial feedback from special education teachers and parents has been highly practical. Special thanks to Jelena Zilic and her children, who provided the first useful in-game test users’ feedback. They helped us see that situations, which are difficult to explain verbally, can become much easier when they are shown visually and practiced through a game. For example, instead of simply telling someone not to respond to a stranger online, SafeClick lets them see the message, decide what to do, and practice blocking and reporting that individual, and reporting the situation to a caregiver. I really believe we managed to turn an abstract topic into something young people can actually practice. GV: How has your own knowledge, awareness, and experience with digital democracy and civic space changed? SF: Before this project, we mostly thought about accessibility as a product and UX (interface) issue. Working on SafeClick made us look at it differently. Being able to use the internet safely is also about being able to participate in everyday life. Communicate, learn, find information, and be part of your community. If a person cannot understand or safely use digital services, they are left out. We also learned that privacy and accessibility should not be things added at the end of development. They need to be considered from the beginning. That is something we will take with us into our future projects. GV: What are the most valuable lessons and experiences you are taking away from this project? SF: The biggest lesson for us was that making something technically simple is actually quite difficult. With commercial products, it is easy to keep adding features. With SafeClick, we had to constantly ask ourselves whether a button, animation, sentence, or screen was really necessary. Our earlier experience with Eureka – Edukativna igra and Lea & Leo helped us understand the value of video games for learning, but SafeClick taught us much more about cognitive accessibility and designing with educators and users in mind. GV: What comes next? How will you apply the learning and digital capacity you have built in your future work and within your community? SF: Our immediate objective is to publish SafeClick, launch it in the media, and inform the wider community about the game’s availability. Looking ahead, we plan to build on this experience to develop a wider portfolio of digital tools tailored for marginalized groups and to continue exploring how games and other digital tools can make learning and participation easier for people who are often left out of mainstream technology. We are open to new collaborations and partnerships. Written by Nurbek Bekmurzaev

title: Complementary forces: Why activism needs art to drive action
description: "Artistic activism uses the emotional experience of art as a prompt for action and directs that action towards change, turning a complex problem into a clear public message."
content: ‘A striking action, a touch of humor, or an unexpected scene can attract attention.’ Originally published on Global Voices An urban art piece called “The Post is fast, it's only the letters that arrive slowly” in front of the main Post Office in Skopje, North Macedonia. This post is by Nikola Pisarev, an art historian and a pioneer of creative activism in North Macedonia, who serves as the program director at the Contemporary Art Center in Skopje . It is also part of Global Voices’ September 2026 Spotlight series, “ Protest in Democracy .” You can support this coverage by donating here . In recent decades, practices that bring art directly into people’s everyday lives have become increasingly common. They may be initiated by artists, activists, informal groups, or citizens who use creative means to draw attention to a problem, express disagreement, or call for change. Public spaces become a place where an action meets an audience, provokes a response, and starts a conversation. This approach, when artistic and creative means are used to press for solutions or encourage social change, is called artistic activism. The “Monument to Diazepam” raised awareness about overuse of prescription drugs. Photo by Nikola Pisarev. Used with permission. At their core, art and activism have different but complementary roles. Activism seeks to change a situation through strategic planning and advocacy; art, on the other hand, is not pro or against but can move people emotionally. Art can change how people see and experience a situation. It opens up new perspectives and associations, and its effects are not always immediate or easy to measure. Artistic activism brings these possibilities together: It uses the emotional experience of art as a prompt for action and directs that action towards change. Urban art actions in North Macedonia offer local examples for exploring this approach. Many actions were developed through direct engagement with specific problems, rather than as part of a broader methodology. They began with a desire to point out an injustice , raise a question, or help address a problem. Urban art action “Fishing for Potholes” in Veles, North Macedonia, which included public performance and distribution of photo and video coverage. Photo by Nikola Pisarev. Used with permission. What makes artistic activism compelling? It does not always take a large crowd to draw attention to a problem. A striking action, a touch of humor, or an unexpected scene can attract attention even when it is created by a small group — or by a single person. This does not replace the power of mass organizing, but it makes action possible when resources are limited. Additionally, amid the constant barrage of information, an unusual sculpture, a witty message, or an intervention in public space can interrupt people’s routine scrolling. They may photograph and share the action, extending its reach beyond the place where it took place through social media and communication platforms. Still, a high number of views does not mean the problem has been solved. Visibility is an opportunity that needs to be connected to the action’s purpose. Within high-risk or authoritarian contexts, creative action can also give activists greater room to act, even under pressure. Humor, metaphor, and unexpected forms can sometimes make a problem visible without direct confrontation. In some cases, the people behind an action can also remain anonymous. This does not make them immune to pressure: The level of risk depends on the context, the subject, and the way the action is carried out. But a creative form may allow organizers to absorb some of that pressure while keeping the affected community less exposed. Likewise, a problem hidden in reports, procedures, or individual experiences can remain invisible to the larger public. An artistic action can translate a complex situation into an image, object, or scene that people can readily recognize. This can encourage citizens, experts and decision-makers to discuss the problem and possible solutions. The challenge is to make the message clear without distorting the substance of the issue. Art also has a way of enduring long after it has disappeared from public space. A scene, symbol, or object can become a story that the media and the public continue to share after the intervention has ended. The people behind an action do not need to specialize in every aspect of the problem. They do need to understand its core, use reliable information, and listen to those directly affected. There are countless ways artistic activism can affect a community. It might prompt an immediate response from the authorities, change how people see an issue, or encourage other social actors to get involved. Immediate response and problem-solving Satirical plaque, supposedly from the Guinness Book of Records for the “World Record for the Longest Road Construction” for an street in Skopje that laid unfinished for years. Photo by Nikola Pisarev. Used with permission. Some actions prompt the authorities to respond quickly. This most often happens with concrete local infrastructure problems: potholes , broken streetlights, faults in water or electricity networks, and smaller environmental issues. North Macedonia has seen many examples: “The Guinness World Record for the Longest Road Construction”; rubber ducklings placed in the mud at the entrance to a kindergarten in Štip; “fishing” for potholes in Veles ; a celebration of the first birthday of a landslide near Kratovo; and the swan lake protest in Orhid . These actions made the situation visible and helped bring about solutions. However, street art actions can also address wider issues, such as personal data protection , disinformation threats , or corruption . Changing views and perceptions Some problems are treated as untouchable, while expert and activist explanations can struggle to reach a wider public. Artistic activism can bridge that gap through the accessibility of an artwork: A simple, readable form can make serious phenomena and policies easier to grasp, encouraging people to question views they may previously have accepted or failed to notice. Simple Styrofoam fins simulated sharks in the Vardar River in the center of Skopje, next to buildings in the shape of sailing ships made as part of Skopje 2014 project . Photo by Nikola Pisarev. Used with permission. Some famous examples of street art activism in North Macedonia include “Sharks in the Vardar River,” which commented on the Skopje 2014 project ; “The Eyes of the Trees,” about excessive tree-cutting in Skopje; the “Monument to Diazepam” to raise awareness about overuse of prescription drugs; the Ohrid trout’s speech for St. Nicholas Day; the giant nest carrying a message from birds; and the campaign for the referendum to save GTC, the historic public City Shopping Center in Skopje . Using different approaches, these actions invited citizens to reconsider their views on public policies and decisions. Added art warns about the plight of the trees. Photo by Nikola Pisarev. Used with permission. Encouraging public responses and broader engagement Some actions aim to provoke responses and mobilize a range of actors. These include not only authorities and institutions, but also professional associations, specialist non-governmental organizations and other groups working on specific issues. At times, such groups may engage less often with the problems citizens face, because communication with communities is limited or because they are reluctant to leave their comfort zones. The media play an important role in this process. Prompted by an action, they seek answers from different actors. When answers are not forthcoming, pressure grows on those actors to take the problem more seriously. In this way, public attention and media coverage can encourage wider engagement. A “clean air cabin” ironically offering “fresh mountain air” in the city of Skopje, which suffers from excessive pollution. Photo by Nikola Pisarev. Used with permission. Early actions on air pollution in Skopje in 2010 and 2011 are one example. With media support, the group “Urban Art Actions” pressured environmental organizations to take air pollution more seriously. A similar approach appears in “ Bread for All ” about poverty; “ How Many More Victims? ” about cyclist safety in Skopje; and more recent actions on river pollution (featuring a mobile statue of floating feces ). In these cases, public pressure helped bring the issues to greater attention among organizations and the wider public. Some of artistic activism’s effectiveness comes from the way actions are made. Preparation often takes place in a studio or garage. It requires serious effort, but can also be an engaging and creative process. Working this way may help people avoid some of the burnout associated with sustained activism, although it does not remove the pressures that can come with public action. Another source of artistic activism’s effectiveness — and one reason it is becoming more visible in public communication — is its ability to make a problem difficult to ignore. When that happens, the political cost of inaction can rise. Authorities may begin to view a problem in terms of its potential effect on voters at the next election. If the cost of addressing it is lower than, or comparable to, the possible loss of votes, a response and a solution become more likely. Written by Guest Contributor

title: After flood disasters, Nepal needs clear numbers on aid and a reconstruction plan
description: Nepal’s flood-hit communities face a long road to recovery as damaged infrastructure, lost livelihoods, and questions over aid transparency complicate efforts to rebuild homes, restore services, and livelihoods.
content: Nepali communities live in the shadow of natural hazards, where uncertainty and fear are daily realities Originally published on Global Voices Settlements across the Tadi River, Devighat in Nuwakot District. Image via Susmita Aryal on October 7, 2026. Used with permission. Forty-six days later, just when Nepal was trying to recover from the Bhotekoshi flash flood , which struck the Nepal–Tibet border regions, affecting Rasuwa and Nuwakot, another landslide-induced flood hit Chumnubri, Gorkha, on October 11, 2026. This latest disaster has added to the wounds of communities who live in the shadow of natural hazards, where uncertainty and fear are daily realities. Read more: The day after the central Nepal flood The climate-related disaster in Nuwakot has devastated a once-popular tourist landscape, destroying its natural beauty and economic opportunities, with settlements heartbreakingly reduced to rubble and vital infrastructure , including roads, bridges and hydro-power facilities, washed away. The full death toll remains officially unconfirmed. Survivors still come to search for their belongings in Devighatm, Nuwakot District. Image via Susmita Aryal on October 7, 2026. Used with permission. But an uncomfortable truth lies behind the devastation: The human cost of such disasters often goes ignored. Behind the statistics are stories of broken dreams, lost livelihoods, buried memories. There are families trying to stay alive without their loved ones, communities faced with an uncertain future, and countless people trying to make lives reconnect and rebuild from what little is left. Read more: Nepal floods: Reporter’s diary, August 27, 2026 The task of rebuilding is huge. The damage is not only to homes, roads and bridges, but also to farms and local businesses. Kyodo News reports via AP that 7,500 homes were damaged or completely destroyed, with costs of recovery hitting USD 4.77 billion. The government has now moved from emergency relief to rehabilitation and reconstruction and has also acknowledged the risks posed by possible glacial outburst floods ( GLOFs ) and other hazards. The destruction of bridges and transport links has made surviving communities vulnerable and slowed reconstruction, exposing residents to further risk. Buildings left standing, and homes left empty in the Bidur Municipality in Nuwakot District. Image via Susmita Aryal on October 7, 2026. Used with permission. To this end, joint efforts are underway to rebuild damaged infrastructure and restore vital services. But pledged assistance is not the same as money that has actually been received and delivered to affected communities. Nepal’s Ministry of Finance’s foreign assistance tracker shows that Nepal has received USD 24.89 million in disaster relief funds. Such tracking can help bring transparency to the collection and distribution of aid. The Prime Minister's Office separately reported that USD 50.47 million of assistance (cash, materials, and teams) had been pledged. No formal update has been given on the implementation of longer-term reconstruction plans. Most of the aid is still going to meet immediate needs like medical aid, food, and temporary shelters, such as tents. What are houses without their people called? Photo featuring reporter Susmita Aryal. Photo from Bidur Municipality in Nuwakot District via Maya Devi Aryal on October 7, 2026. Used with permission. Many affected communities remain far from rebuilt infrastructure and restored livelihoods. India, China, the United States, and the United Arab Emirates (UAE) are providing assistance, and the Asian Development Bank and other international financial institutions have committed funds . Yet recovery is likely to progress unevenly. The challenge for affected communities is not just to rebuild what was lost but to restore livelihoods, public services and a sense of security in the face of recurring environmental hazards. In the following photo essay, Global Voices highlights how Nepali citizens are still affected by the disaster. All photos were taken by Susmita Aryal in Bidur Municipality, Nuwakot District on October 7, 2026. Tara Devi Tamang and others waiting for relief and basic needs provided at the Bidur Municipality Office, Nuwakot District. Image via Susmita Aryal. Used with permission Daily essentials scattered around the community in Bidur Municipality in Nuwakot District. Image via Susmita Aryal. Used with permission. A half-destroyed shelter once used to be a home. Photo from Bidur Municipality in Nuwakot District. Image via Susmita Aryal. Used with permission. Somebody’s whole world reduced to rubble. Image from Bidur Municipality in Nuwakot District via Susmita Aryal. Used with permission. A viral house broken window pane weaponized for an emergency flight. Image from Bidur Municipality in Nuwakot District via Susmita Aryal. Used with permission. Nothing is left of a riverside home in Bidur Municipality in Nuwakot District. Image via Susmita Aryal. Used with permission. A helmet sits alone without its rider. Image from Bidur Municipality in Nuwakot District via Susmita Aryal. Used with permission. Written by Susmita Aryal

title: Poetry book promotes Chabacano, Asia’s only Spanish-based creole language
description: "The project highlights not only the continued vitality of Chavacano as a language, but also the efforts of its speakers to create new literature and preserve the language through writing.”
content: Ten authors and 23 poems are featured in the anthology Originally published on Global Voices Photo from the Facebook page of Voces del Alma. Used with permission A new poetry anthology features writers of Chabacano, one of the Philippines’ 170 languages, which is widely spoken in the southernmost city of Zamboanga, and stands out as Asia’s only Spanish-based creole language. The Philippines was a colony of Spain for more than three centuries, but the Spanish language was only used by the elite, friars, and colonial rulers. Only in Zamboanga did a Spanish-based creole language develop. In 2018, Global Voices featured Bien Chabacano , a blog dedicated to promoting and documenting Chavacano de Zamboanga. Its creator, Jerome Herrera, launched a book project this year by inviting writers to submit poems to be compiled in an anthology. This led to the launch of the “ Sombra y Luz ” book in July, featuring 23 poems by 10 authors. The poems are mainly about love, family, and Zamboangueño identity. Herrera said , “The project highlights not only the continued vitality of Chavacano as a literary language, but also the efforts of its speakers to create new literature and preserve the language through writing.” He added that the book title aims to convey a message of contrast about the changes in Zamboanga City. The book cover also provides a nostalgic reference to the flowers that decorated the city in the past. The cover features an American-era style lamppost that can be seen along the Zamboanga boulevard. The cover also features bougainvilleas which my dad tells me were ubiquitous in Zamboanga City back when it was known as the Ciudad de Flores. One of the poems in the anthology, written by Jayline Gonzales-Barredo, mentions flowers and birds that enrich life in the city. Maga pajaro que ta vola-vola, Na maga rama de pono ta queda, Alegre con uno y otro ta grita-grita, Twit! Twit! Twit! Entero el dia. Mio pueblo Ciudad de Zamboanga, Ciudad de Flores que llama. De noche mucho pajaro ay columbra, Na maga cable de corriente ta esta. Birds that fly and flutter freely, Perched upon the branches of trees, Singing and calling each other joyfully, Tweet! Tweet! Tweet! All day long. Oh, my beloved City of Zamboanga, City of Flowers, they call you. At night, many birds can be found, Sitting on wires, that’s what they do. In an interview with Global Voices, Herrera noted the heavy use of Spanish words in the selected poems: …there is a lot of debate with regards to what Chabacano poetry should look like. For some, they like it with a lot of Spanish words and for others, they like it to be exactly as how Chabacano appears in everyday conversations. Most of the poems submitted leaned heavily on Spanish words, I think primarily because Chabacano writers rely on Spanish words to make their works sound more formal as well as more poetic. Since it’s poetry, I thought that it was alright to present Chabacano in an idealistic manner. He added that the anthology seeks to encourage more people to accept the various ways that Chabacano is used. For a very long time, people have been putting Chabacano inside a box. I hope that these books open up conversations regarding Chabacano literature and make people receptive to different kinds of writing styles in Chabacano. This approach is evident in the poem “Escribi Chavacano, Conversa Chabacano,” which celebrates Chabacano as a living language. Through references to poems, essays, fables, and the stories passed down by elders, the author reminds readers that the language continues to thrive when it is written, spoken, and shared with others. The title itself is noteworthy for its use of both Chavacano and Chabacano, reflecting the coexistence of two accepted spellings of the language. In doing so, the poem highlights not only the importance of preserving Chabacano, but also the richness and diversity of its written tradition. View this post on Instagram Herrera’s interview with Asymptote Journal noted the challenge of finding Chabacano contributors, and his hope that the book project can lead to more literary initiatives. The biggest challenge is keeping the momentum going, since it’s hard to find Chavacano poets. Even so, I hope this anthology is just the beginning and that we’ll be able to publish a second volume in the future. Written by Mong Palatino

title: What African elections can learn from the Borana Gadaa system
description: Discover how the Borana Gadaa system can inspire African elections through peaceful power transitions, accountable leadership, inclusive governance, and traditional democratic practices that strengthen public trust and participation.
content: Can the Borana Gadaa system inspire fairer elections, peaceful transitions, and stronger democracy across Africa? Originally published on Global Voices A Balli Walirafudhu handover ceremony held by the Borana Oromo people in Southern Ethiopia and northern Kenya. They have long practiced rotational, peaceful leadership transfer, known as the Borana Gadaa system. Photo used with permission. This article by Diba Kosi Bilinga was originally published by Peace News Network on July 20, 2026. An edited version is being republished on Global Voices under a content partnership agreement. Every election season, much of Africa braces itself. In some cases, incumbents amend constitutions to erase term limits, and citizens wait to see whether power will change hands at the ballot box or in the streets. The pattern repeats: disputed results , ethnic mobilization, coups , or leaders who refuse to leave . Yet in the rangelands of southern Ethiopia and northern Kenya, the Borana Oromo people have long practiced rotational, peacefully transferred leadership. Known as the Borana Gadaa system, UNESCO inscribed it in 2016 as an Intangible Cultural Heritage of Humanity that regulates political and social life, resolves conflict, and protects women’s rights. This article asks a question: What can African leaders, electoral commissions, political parties, and citizens learn from a governance model that has quietly rotated power every eight years for generations, without coups, without third-term referenda, and without the bloodshed that so often accompanies modern African elections? Lesson 1: Power must have a time limit Borana leadership rotates on a fixed eight-year cycle among five Gogeessas (parties). Each governs for one Gadaa period, then hands over power, returning to the first after 40 years — a rotation built into the structure itself. Compare this to Africa’s modern pattern. Human Rights Watch (HRW) director Ida Sawyer describes a “constitutional coup” pattern: leaders who cannot win re-election simply rewrite the laws to get their way. Cameroon’s Paul Biya erased term limits in 2008 and has ruled since 1982; Uganda’s Museveni scrapped his in 2005 ; Rwanda, Burundi, Togo, Djibouti, and the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC) have each amended their constitutions to extend a president’s tenure. Gadaa’s lesson is structural: When a time limit is built into the system itself, rather than a leader’s promise, departure never has to be settled by force. Lesson 2: Prepare leaders before giving them power Gadaa systems treat leadership as something built over decades, not switched on by an election. Members pass through age-grades from childhood, absorbing law, custom, and ritual responsibility long before they are eligible to lead — knowledge oral historians formally transmit across generations. Most African political systems do the opposite: Candidates are selected first, and asked whether they are fit to govern only afterward. Patronage, money, and ethnic arithmetic often outweigh demonstrated understanding of law or public finance, producing leaders who improvise governance while learning on the job. The lesson for African parties and civic institutions: Build structured pipelines — in local councils, youth wings, and civil service — that expose future leaders to responsibility long before a national mandate. Lesson 3: Peaceful transitions are a sign of institutional strength, not weakness Under the Gadaa system, at the Balli Walirafudhu handover ceremony, authority passes from the outgoing ruling class to the incoming one, understood by the whole community as final and binding. Every eight years, the Gumi Gaayo assembly , held under the sacred Odaa tree, reviews the era’s laws and blesses the incoming leadership. Contrast that with Kenya’s 2007 to 08 crisis, when a disputed result triggered ethnic violence that killed roughly 1,000 people and displaced 500,000, per HRW’s investigation . Ivory Coast saw a similar rupture in 2010 to 2011, leading to a civil war . In the Borana Gadaa system, succession is scripted years in advance. In much of Africa, it is an open question resolved only after votes are contested. Lesson 4: No clan or ethnicity should own the political system The Borana society has two broad blocks, the Sabboo Sadeen clan and the Goonaa Bal’aa clan, each with its own sub-clans. But the five Gogeessa that hold political authority cut across these clan lines — political identity and clan identity stay separate, so no single clan can capture the system. This fault line has broken many African elections. The violence in Kenya in 2007 to 2008 was driven largely by ethnic mobilization, with the Center for Strategic and International Studies ( CSIS ) noting ethnicity as the main axis political elites mobilize around — turning elections into an ethnic census. Where political identity is inseparable from ethnicity, losing an election can feel like losing everything for a whole community. Gadaa’s design offers a template: build structures — party membership, constituencies, civil-service recruitment — that mix identities rather than reinforce them. Lesson 5: Democracy is more than voting day Gadaa’s Gumi Gaayo assembly does far more than confirm who leads. It reviews the era’s laws, arbitrates disputes, and holds outgoing leaders publicly accountable — through consultation among elders and councils of advisors (Hayyuu), not a ballot cast once every few years. Much of Africa’s politics concentrates almost all democratic energy into a single day. ITUC-Africa cataloged disputed results across Guinea, Togo, Sudan, Burundi, Burkina Faso, Egypt, Comoros, Tanzania, and Rwanda in 2010 alone — accountability between elections proved far weaker than the contest itself. Robust democracies need standing institutions — independent courts, electoral commissions, a free press and community dispute-resolution bodies — that keep working every day of the cycle. Lesson 6: Leadership should serve the institution, not the other way around The Abbaa Gadaa — the topmost Borana Leader — never rules alone. He operates alongside the Hayyuu council of advisors, the Abbaa Seera responsible for law, and the ritual authority of the Qaalluu — a deliberately decentralized structure, as one account puts it, designed to stop any office from concentrating too much power. Across Africa, the opposite dominates. A 2026 survey found rulers such as Cameroon’s Paul Biya (in power since 1982), Equatorial Guinea’s Teodoro Obiang Nguema Obiang (since 1979) and Congo’s Sassou Nguesso (since 1979) have systematically dismantled the checks meant to constrain them. In each case, the presidency grew larger than the constitution meant to contain it. When power is distributed across councils, courts, and customary bodies, no single leader’s ambition can capture the whole state. Lesson 7: Resolve conflict through dialogue before It becomes violence Borana layers its conflict resolution: The Kora Gossa handles local clan disputes, the Gumi Gaayo settles national matters, and Boran Haraamu Koo’puu Rules — a form of social exclusion — is reserved for those who break the community’s deepest trust. Modern West Africa shows what happens when such mediation is absent. Since 2020, the Sahel has seen a wave of takeovers — Mali, Guinea, Burkina Faso, Niger, Gabon — linked to deteriorating security and falling accountability in the years before each coup. The lesson is not that customary courts should replace constitutions, but that no state can survive on election-day mechanisms alone — it needs everyday channels of mediation to build citizens’ trust. Lesson 8: Culture, memory, and inclusion are part of governance Borana Gadaa’s institutions are inseparable from Borana culture. The Odaa tree is both a meeting place and a living symbol of continuity across generations. Knowledge of the system’s history — including a documented line of more than 72 Abbaa Gadaa — is preserved and transmitted by oral historians. Governance needs more than law and procedure — it needs cultural memory, shared symbols, and inclusive channels through which groups historically shut out of power, especially women, can still be heard. African leaders don’t need to build Odaa trees or revive age-grade systems to learn from the Borana Gadaa. They need its underlying logic: time limits built into institutions, leaders prepared long before office, structures that cut across ethnic lines, power distributed across bodies, and dialogue running continuously rather than waiting for crisis. Written by Peace News

title: Bangladesh-Malaysia recruitment reforms revive old questions over the cost of migration
description: Bangladesh and Malaysia have made several government-level agreements for labour migration over the years, but problems such as syndication, excessive recruitment costs and human rights abuses remain unresolved.
content: Repeated disruptions raise concerns over recruitment transparency and migrant workers’ protection from exploitation. Originally published on Global Voices On Saturday, October 5, 2024, a Memorandum of Collaboration (MOC) was signed in Dhaka between the Wage Earners Welfare Board and Malaysia's PERKESO, regarding the expansion of the labor market in Malaysia. Image via Wikipedia by Press Information Department of Bangladesh. Public Domain. Officials in both Bangladesh and Malaysia’s have made repeated attempts to reform the countries’ labour migration relationship, leading to numerous suspensions and reopenings over more than three decades. However, on August 30, 2026, Bangladesh’s State Minister for Local Government, Rural Development and Cooperatives, Mir Shahe Alam, announced that Malaysia would recruit around 200,000 Bangladeshi workers over six months, with departures expected to begin in late September. He also referred to a plan to send 10,000 workers without requiring them to bear migration costs. Two days later, however, Malaysia’s government spokesperson Fahmi Fadzil clarified that the figure of 200,000 workers did not represent an official government position. The clarification introduced fresh uncertainty over the scale and timing of the recruitment drive. The mixed signals came as the two countries were trying to reset a labour migration corridor that has faced repeated allegations of excessive recruitment fees, syndication and worker exploitation. Repeated reopenings, repeated suspensions Bangladesh first entered into an agreement with Malaysia for the systematic transfer of labour in 1992, followed by another agreement in 1994 that provided for the recruitment of 50,000 workers annually, mainly for the construction sector. Between 1992 and 1998, around 307,000 Bangladeshi workers were issued permits to work in Malaysia. But recruitment was halted in 1997 amid a rise in unauthorised migration. During that period, local brokers could charge workers between USD 2,000 (approximately BDT 245,700) and USD 3,000 (approximately BDT 368,600) for authorised migration. In an effort to reduce recruitment malpractice and costs, the two governments turned to a government-to-government model ( G2G model ) in 2012. The programme initially aimed to recruit around 30,000 Bangladeshi workers for Malaysia’s palm-oil sector. More than 1.4 million people registered and workers were selected through a lottery system. The G2G arrangement substantially reduced migration costs, but it struggled to meet its recruitment targets. The system was later replaced by the G2G Plus arrangement. Under the model introduced in 2016, Malaysia selected only 10 Bangladeshi recruiting agencies. Although the agreed migration cost was around BDT 37,000-40,000 (approximately USD 300 to USD 325), later reports put the amount actually paid by workers at an average of around BDT 300,000 to 400,000 (approximately USD 2,450 to USD 3,260). Allegations of syndication, high costs and other irregularities eventually led Malaysia to suspend recruitment again in 2018. Recruitment resumed following a new memorandum of understanding signed in December 2021. Between 2022 and 2024, 476,672 Bangladeshi workers were sent to Malaysia through 101 recruiting agencies. But by June 2024, the labour market had again closed to new Bangladeshi recruits amid concerns over high migration costs and worker exploitation. Against this history of repeated closed and reopened borders, the latest attempt to reset recruitment has revived a familiar question: whether the new arrangement can reduce the financial burden on workers and prevent the problems that undermined earlier recruitment systems. The latest debacle On August 28, 2026, Bangladesh’s Ministry of Expatriates’ Welfare and Overseas Employment outlined a broader recruitment arrangement involving 338 entities. Malaysia had directly selected 25 recruiting agencies, while 312 others were approved to work as associates. The state-run Bangladesh Overseas Employment and Services Limited, or BOESL, was also included. Under the same arrangement, Malaysia had agreed in principle to take 10,000 workers on a zero-cost basis . Prospective migrants were also warned not to make payments, undergo medical examinations or hand over their passports until formal instructions were issued. That warning stands out against the record of the previous recruitment cycle. In July 2026, Bangladesh revoked the licences of 49 recruiting agencies over alleged syndication and irregularities linked to Malaysia-bound recruitment. The Anti-Corruption Commission alleged that agencies under investigation had sent 267,276 workers to Malaysia and collected more than BDT 45.45 billion (approximately USD 370 million) in excess fees. The government-approved recruitment cost was BDT 78,990 (approximately USD 645), yet investigators alleged that some workers were charged as much as five times that amount. Concerns over high recruitment costs have continued into the new cycle, with industry sources warning that migration expenses could exceed BDT 600,000 (approximately USD 4,900). The financial burden is not limited to the Malaysia corridor. Bangladesh’s Labour Force Survey 2024 found that migrant workers spent an average of BDT 463,000 (approximately USD 3,778 ) on recruitment. With average monthly earnings of BDT 42,599 (approximately USD 348), recovering that expense took about 10.9 months on average. For some families, however, the financial loss begins even before a worker leaves Bangladesh. Paying for a journey that never happened For a 22-year-old worker originally from Sherpur, Bangladesh, the financial loss began with a job abroad that he never reached. Speaking to Global Voices by phone and asking to remain anonymous, he said he began preparing to migrate to Malaysia around 2024 after hearing about work opportunities through a local intermediary. By the time the process stalled, his family had spent around BDT 500,000 (approximately USD 4,079). The money came from their savings, the sale of land and loans — around BDT 220,000 (approximately USD 1,795) of which were borrowed at interest. The payments were made in stages for visa processing, medical costs and other expenses. Much of the process was handled through a local intermediary rather than directly with a recruiting agency, and the worker said he did not receive receipts for all of the money he paid. “At first they said it would take two or three months, but six or seven months passed. Whenever I asked for an update, the intermediary gave a different answer but never gave me a clear one. I had already done the medical and submitted my passport. Eventually they told me the Malaysian market had closed and there was nothing more they could do.” By then, however, the full amount had already been paid, leaving him and his family with the financial burden. “I thought I would go to Malaysia, earn money, and repay the loan. But I could not go. I got some of the money back, but they still have not returned the rest. Whenever I call, they just say, ‘Give us some more time.’ I do not know how long I am supposed to keep waiting. I am still here, but I am still paying off the debt I took to go abroad.” The consequences also reached the rest of the household. His mother, who also spoke to Global Voices by phone and asked to remain anonymous, said, “My husband died a long time ago. We only had a small piece of land, so I sold it. I also borrowed money with interest and somehow managed the rest for my son. I thought that if he could go abroad and earn well, we would repay everything. But he could not go. Now we still have to keep paying the interest, whether we have enough for food or not.” A wider pattern of recruitment debt The family’s experience sits within a broader pattern of high recruitment costs and debt among Bangladeshis seeking work in Malaysia. Research by Verité , an independent nonprofit organization advancing fair labor worldwide, on the Bangladesh–Malaysia migration corridor found that workers paid an average of about USD 5,000 (approximately BDT 614,400) in recruitment-related costs, often financing the journey through multiple loans. Among the workers surveyed , 73 percent spent at least half of their monthly salary on recruitment debt, while 43 percent reported wage deception. The role of intermediaries has also been identified as a major driver of those costs. An International Organization for Migration (IOM) study on recruitment practices in Bangladesh found that aspiring migrants often rely on sub-agents and informal intermediaries because they have little direct contact with recruiting agencies or do not fully understand the formal process. The study identified reducing the unauthorised involvement of such intermediaries as a key step towards lowering migration costs. A separate IOM study on migrant debt found that limited information about official migration channels can push prospective workers towards intermediaries who charge high fees. It also identified limited access to formal finance and legal remedies as factors that can deepen migrant indebtedness. What remains unclear in the new recruitment cycle As Bangladesh and Malaysia move towards restarting recruitment, key details of the process remain unsettled. By September 30, 2026, the Bangladesh High Commission in Kuala Lumpur had begun attesting job-demand letters, but the government had yet to announce the final recruitment cost, departure timeline, or full procedure. Expatriates’ Welfare and Overseas Employment Minister Ariful Haque Chowdhury said an official announcement would be made soon. The structure of the new arrangement has also drawn criticism from within the recruitment industry. Some Bangladesh Association of International Recruiting Agencies ( BAIRA ) members argued that the 312 associate agencies should have direct access to Malaysia’s Foreign Workers Centralised Management System rather than relying on the 25 principal agencies to process workers. Other recruiters rejected concerns about renewed syndication, saying associate agencies could still obtain job demand and recruit workers. In November 2025, UN human rights experts expressed renewed concern over the continued exploitation, deception and deepening debt bondage of Bangladeshi migrant workers in Malaysia. They called on both governments to investigate reported abuses, provide effective remedies including restitution and debt relief, strengthen oversight of recruitment practices and cooperate to dismantle exploitative recruitment networks. The recruitment corridor has also faced repeated suspensions amid recurring allegations of syndication, excessive recruitment costs and worker exploitation. Malaysia suspended recruitment of Bangladeshi workers in 2018 following controversy surrounding the limited-agency system, and again in June 2024 amid concerns over excessive migration costs and workers arriving without jobs. The repeated disruptions have renewed concerns over whether restricted recruitment arrangements can ensure transparency and protect workers from exploitation. Meanwhile, the Malaysian government has warned agencies not to collect money or passports before formal instructions are issued. Migration researcher Shariful Hasan also told The Daily Star that any reopening should clearly establish who controls recruitment, how much workers are required to pay and who is accountable when problems arise. Bangladesh and Malaysia have made several government-level agreements over the years, but problems such as syndication, excessive recruitment costs and human rights abuses remain unresolved. Remittances are a major source of support for Bangladesh’s economy, yet migrant workers continue to bear significant human and financial costs. This highlights the need for urgent reforms by both governments that are transparent and centred on the rights and protection of workers. Written by Maksuda Akter

title: When free speech has a price: Youth voices in Mozambique
description: For Mozambican youth, freedom of expression exists in law, but speaking out can come with a cost. Music became a powerful space for criticism and resistance.
content: When speaking freely can have a cost, young people turn to music to challenge political silence Originally published on Global Voices A group of men during a peaceful protest; one of them holds a microphone and a banner. Photo taken by Stephanie Douglas. Nigeria. Via Pexels . Pexels License . In Mozambique , freedom of expression is regulated by the Law on the Right to Information No. 34/2014 , a constitutionally guaranteed right under Article 48 of the Constitution of the Republic of Mozambique . However, for many young people, speaking publicly about corruption, inequality, police violence, or accountability continues to carry risk, showing the gap between the promises of democracy and actual daily experience. In music, for example, this contradiction is clear. Over the past two decades, hip-hop has become a key space for urban youth to voice social criticism, particularly in the capital city, Maputo . More than simply a musical genre, hip-hop became a way of documenting the concerns of a generation that grew up with, on one hand, political democratization and multipartyism from the early 1990s , but on the other, high youth unemployment, economic inequalities, and growing distrust in public institutions led by the ruling FRELIMO party. Through musical narratives, groups like GPRO and artists like Azagaia created a language that reflected people’s daily experiences in public and institutional spaces. Perhaps the question Azagaia poses in the song “ O ciclo da Censura ” (Cycle of Censorship) remains relevant: “Who said that in this country there is freedom of expression?” This is not just a provocative artistic comment. It is a reflection on the material and political conditions that determine who can speak, about what, and with what consequences. New forms of citizenship Mozambican youth have been reinventing ways of participating politically. While for many years citizenship was strongly associated with political parties and state organizations, today it also flows through other organizations such as feminist collectives like the Woman’s Forum , digital platforms for monitoring local governance , cultural associations, and artistic initiatives. This change points to a generation that does not accept politics being limited to elections, and demands the right to continually participate in the shaping of public spaces. However, these new forms of participation often conflict with authorities that continue to view protest as a threat to public order. One of the most striking events happened in 2016, when feminist organizations took to the streets to protest the banning of miniskirts in state schools . The measure was presented as a response to sexual harassment, but it implied that female students’ clothing choices were the cause of the harm they suffered. By holding the girls accountable instead of the aggressors, the debate revealed something deeper: the dispute over control of the female body and the right of young women to define their own identity. During the demonstrations, the Spanish activist Eva Anadón Moreno was detained and subsequently expelled from Mozambique for participating in the protest. Silence is also political In recent years, censorship in Mozambique has rarely come in the form of explicit prohibitions. However, that does not mean that fear and self-censorship are entirely absent. In a 2010 interview, Azagaia observed that the biggest obstacle to freedom of expression in Mozambique was not necessarily direct police intimidation, but rather economic precarity. When many job opportunities depend, directly or indirectly, on relationships with established power structures, public criticism can put people at risk. This results in what could be called the “economy of silence.” Journalists avoid certain topics, artists moderate what they say, public officials keep their opinions quiet, and young activists learn that words can carry a high cost. Freedom then ceases to be merely a legal issue and becomes a matter of survival. In this context, protest music takes on a particular political value. It breaks the collective silence and develops communities of recognition-building, where experiences of injustice find language, memory, and solidarity. The mirage of freedom of expression The Mozambican Constitution affirms the right of all citizens to freedom of expression and opinion. But a democracy is not measured only by rights on paper, but also by the real conditions in which they can be exercised. The mirage of freedom lies in this contradiction: Citizens are asked to believe they can speak freely, while informal mechanisms of surveillance, stigmatization, and exclusion limit who can participate in public space. It is not necessary to prohibit all voices; it is enough to make the costs of dissent intimidatingly high, such as, for example, the increase of telecommunications tariffs above the real cost . In this context, the youth activism symbolizes this ambivalence. They amplify historically marginalized voices and make them more visible. The greater the capacity of an artist, activist, or youth collective to mobilize people, the greater the risk of intimidation, disinformation, or economic isolation. Amplifying youth voices Despite the challenges, youth continue to create new forms of political hope. Art, music, and digital activism show that citizenship is not just a legal status, but a daily practice of participation, imagination, and resistance. The real challenge of protecting Mozambicans is not just freedom of expression as written in the constitution, but creating conditions for everybody to exercise it without fear of economic, social, or political reprisals. The fundamental question for Mozambique is not just whether young people can speak, but whether they can speak without putting their safety, their job, or their ability to participate in public life at risk. Written (Português) by Tirso Sitoe Translated (English) by Liam Anderson View original post (Português)

title: How Ecuador is fighting to keep industrial trans fats off the food shelf
description: As health advocates push for tighter controls, Ecuador confronts the gap between regulating trans fats and enforcing those rules.
content: A public health battle over what ends up on Ecuador’s food shelves Originally published on Global Voices Civil society, academia, and the State met in Quito to discuss progress toward the regulation of trans fatty acids in a country where non-communicable diseases account for more than 76% of deaths. Photo by Salomé Rosales Estrella/Minga por la Pachamama, 2026. Used with permission. “What are we eating? Foods that regenerate or products that degenerate life?” asked Eliana Estrella on September 7, 2026, in the auditorium of Universidad San Francisco de Quito in Ecuador. The popular communicator and member of the Committee of Users of the Food Market (CUUM) was speaking at the Hearts Free of Trans Fats meeting, before social organizations, academia and health agencies. The event was the first activity in a packed three-day agenda. On September 8, civic organizations and representatives of academia met at FLACSO Ecuador for the workshop “Adding Voices for Health: Ecuador Meeting 2026,” dedicated to identifying priorities, capacities and advocacy strategies regarding noncommunicable diseases, while on September 10, the discussion “Food for Life” examined the responses promoted by civil society, their difficulties and their challenges. Estrella’s question brought the discussion back to an everyday scene: a person standing in front of a shelf. Products like margarines, cookies, spreads, doughnuts, cakes and some fried foods may contain industrial trans fats , and depend on the oils, fats and processes used to make them — a difference that is not always evident when making a choice. The World Health Organization (WHO) explains that these fats are produced mainly through partial hydrogenation: hydrogen is added to a liquid oil to make it solid or semi-solid.
